#10031. Introducing Real World VoiceEQ: Measuring the human quality of voice AI

Existing benchmarks suggest voice AI is nearing human-level performance but real-world conversations tell a different story.

Voice is rapidly becoming AI's primary interface. From customer support and healthcare to education, entertainment, and personal assistants, speech is increasingly replacing text as the way people interact with AI.

Over the last few years, voice models have improved dramatically. Word error rates continue to fall, latency has reached conversational speeds, and many established benchmarks are approaching saturation. Yet anyone who regularly uses voice AI knows something still feels off.

Voice models can sound like different people over the course of a conversation, miss hesitation or uncertainty, and struggle with accents, noise, or emotional speech. Those shortcomings are easy to miss in benchmarks focused on latency and word error rate. People care whether a voice system can truly listen, respond appropriately, and remain natural and reliable in real conversations.

To measure those qualities, we built Real World VoiceEQ—a benchmark designed to evaluate the human quality of voice interaction. It assesses whether voice systems can recognize, produce, and respond to the acoustic information transcripts leave out, from tone and emotion to speaker identity and background context.

Real World VoiceEQ evaluates more than 40 leading proprietary and open-source voice models across 15+ key evaluation dimensions and more than 60 metrics spanning Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR), Text-to-Speech (TTS), Speech-to-Speech (S2S), and Speech Understanding.

Real World VoiceEQ was developed from more than 1 million individual human ratings collected across different demographics, speaking styles, and acoustic environments. The current benchmark includes 785,000 TTS ratings and 48,000 STS ratings, making it one of the largest human evaluations of voice AI conducted to date.

Every evaluation was conducted using Kairos, our flexible, voice-native evaluation platform. The same infrastructure enables frontier AI labs and enterprises to run custom evaluations tailored to specific use cases, identify granular failure modes in production voice systems, generate human preference data, and continuously improve models through reinforcement learning and human feedback.

The race for a single "best" voice model is giving way to a collection of specialized capabilities.

Today's leading systems optimize for different strengths—including technical accuracy, emotional understanding, conversational intelligence, expressiveness, and robustness. One model that excels at repeating booking reference numbers, bank account details, or complex pharmaceutical names may struggle to produce emotionally expressive speech. Another may sound remarkably natural but be less reliable on precision-oriented tasks.

As voice AI matures, measuring progress increasingly requires evaluating these capabilities independently rather than collapsing them into a single overall score. In our TTS evaluations, no system configuration ranked among the top five across all eight capability groups—underscoring why there is no single "best" voice model.

Speech-to-Speech models showed the widest variation of any category we evaluated. Some systems recognized emotion exceptionally well but struggled to respond naturally. We found that access to audio did not guarantee that agents used the paralinguistic information it contained. Some systems remained largely transcript-driven, relying on the words being spoken while overlooking cues such as tone, pacing, hesitation, emphasis, and volume.

Humans naturally use these cues to infer confidence, uncertainty, frustration, sarcasm, and empathy. Today's models often miss them.

Imagine a banking agent asking whether you recognize a potentially fraudulent transaction. A confident "Yes" and a hesitant "…yes…" may have completely different meanings, even though the transcript is identical. Humans recognize that difference immediately. Many of today's voice models do not.

Many established benchmarks are nearing their limits and don't reflect real-world conditions. Models still struggle with accented speech, overlapping speakers, emotion, background noise, and longer conversations. In our evaluation, performance varies far more across leading open-source and proprietary models than traditional benchmarks suggest. In one example, transcription word error rates on noise-backed speech were roughly four times higher than on music-backed speech, showing how a single background-audio score can hide the real failure mode.

In preliminary research, we found signs that some models may be optimized for established public benchmarks. Several reproduced known errors in reference transcripts, followed arbitrary spelling conventions, and even reconstructed masked words that were not present in the audio.

LLMs are now widely used to evaluate text-based models, but our findings suggest that speech-language models (SLMs) should be used more carefully for voice evaluation. When we compared leading SLMs with trained human raters on text-to-speech assessments, agreement was highest on tasks with clear, verifiable answers, such as pronunciation accuracy.

Agreement declined on more subjective evaluations. SLMs sometimes appeared to infer emotion from text-based contextual cues, and agreement was weakest for open-ended judgments such as whether a voice fit an acting role or maintained a consistent identity. Automated evaluators can be valuable for well-defined tasks, but they are not yet a substitute for human listeners when judgments depend on acoustic-context, perception, and social interpretation.

As voice becomes one of AI's defining interfaces, speed and technical accuracy alone will no longer determine which systems succeed. The models people ultimately choose will be those that can understand, express, and respond like humans—not just under ideal benchmark conditions, but across the complexity of real-world conversation.

For decades, speech AI has advanced by optimizing against quantitative metrics on standardized benchmarks; from WER for transcription accuracy to objective perceptual metrics like PESQ and DNSMOS for speech quality. We hope Real World VoiceEQ can extend this paradigm by providing a human-grounded metric for evaluating the components of synthetic voice interactions.

Read the full technical report and explore the public leaderboards—or get in touch to learn how Hume can evaluate your voice model or agent using Real World VoiceEQ, or design custom evaluations tailored to your specific use case.

#10030. ChatGPT shrunk down to run on a Super Nintendo

Just don't expect complex, coherent, or always correct answers

If you’ve ever wondered how small an instance of ChatGPT could get, wonder no longer. Someone has actually rigged up a tiny version of the chatbot to run on a Super Nintendo cartridge.

Tech journalist and retro tech enthusiast Benj Edwards is responsible for ChatGPT for SNES. He's published it online running in an emulator, complete with SNES-era music and sound effects, and for download as an SNES ROM, too.

It’s not a big model, mind you, and performance is thus pretty limited: According to the website, it’s a 2.2 million-parameter offshoot of OpenAI’s GPT-OSS-120b, which was used to develop its training conversations – so in that sense it truly is a ChatGPT that runs on an SNES cartridge. Edwards described it to The Register as a distilled version of the aforementioned open-weight model.

There are two options built into ChatGPT for SNES: One that’s purely the model, with every word generated coming right from its tiny little silicon brain, and another that includes a fact book culled from the opening sentences of around 150,000 simple English Wikipedia articles. If you opt to run both versions and ask it the same questions, you’ll notice a massive difference.

Given some of the other responses we got while testing, there’s really no good reason to run the base model – memory isn’t really an issue given the basic build is about 4MB and the factbook build is just 19MB.

Edwards admits that it’s not the most helpful AI model, either – this is just an experiment after all.

“It is not a useful assistant: the model is millions of times smaller than the models behind ChatGPT, knows about 8,000 words, and often gets things wrong, sometimes confidently,” Edwards noted in his writeup. In that sense, it really is vintage AI on vintage hardware. “The fact book can carry mistakes too.”

If you have an SNES lying around (lucky you), you can download the ROM from this link. If you want to get it running on an SNES you’ll need a cartridge that allows running of custom ROMs, and that supports Nintendo’s Super FX graphics coprocessor. Cartridges like the FXPak Pro and SD2SNES support it. The factbook version also requires support for the aftermarket Media Streaming Unit 1 (MSU-1), which adds CD-ROM like features to the SNES. MSU-1 is available in both of the flash carts mentioned above.

If you have some real hardware skills, however, you could technically make your own ChatGPT cartridge.

“The ‘pure’ version, which generates all responses from the AI language model, could run from a real custom SNES cart,” Edwards told us – it doesn’t even actually need the Super FX chip. “I do have a version of ChatGPT for SNES that can run without the Super FX chip, but without the extra processing power the answers are not as good.”

That said, Edwards believes its absolutely crazy and nonsensical answers are part of the fun.

“ChatGPT for SNES can definitely make mistakes too, but it's almost cute when it does it because of its limited knowledge and its playful interface,” Edwards told us.

While a human may have designed the experiment, the coding work was done by AI, Edwards told us – he’s been interested in it since the 1990s and is pursuing more experiments with tiny AI models using the help of the bigger ones.

“I've been theorizing about what I call ‘tiny talking machines’ … over the past year,” Edwards told us, and he’s been able to use coding agents to turn those ideas into actual software. ChatGPT for SNES is one example, and he also created an NES ROM called Séance that uses an even smaller AI model able to run on an original Nintendo Entertainment System that simulates talking to a ghost in a haunted game cartridge.

“I designed the scope of what the software should be, how it should work broadly, what chip it should use, how the interface should look and work, and the sounds it makes when it types responses,” Edwards told us. He added that he sees the project as an AI/human collaboration, which is where he believes AI works best.

“The AI agents who did the coding for this project currently advise that we've hit the limit of how good the AI model can be on the limited hardware,” Edwards said - he’s not taking their word for it, though. “It's up to human creativity to transcend those assumptions. I have already come up with new ideas that I believe can make a tiny model like ChatGPT for SNES even more coherent, and I'm working on them now.” ®

#10028. Welcome Inkling by Thinking Machines

Update: Inkling 2 Small is here! 🤗 Thinking Machines released Inkling 2 Small, the next generation of the Inkling family. We have updated this post with a new section on Inkling 2 Small, covering what changed in the architecture and how to run it with transformers.

Inkling is Thinking Machines' family of open multimodal models, and it now spans two generations on the Hub:

In this post, we start with the first-generation architecture, then walk through what changed in Inkling 2 Small and how to run it. The rest of the post covers inference, use cases, post-training, and deployment, with examples built on the first-generation checkpoints.

Inkling is the first large open model with ~1T parameters and 1M context window to natively receive image, text, and audio inputs, trained on 45 trillion tokens of text, images, audio and video. It’s focused on reasoning across modalities such as audio, images, and text. It is intended for domain adaptation via fine-tuning. We’ve tinkered (pun intended) with this model to build some demos and explore the architecture, and we think it’s great for building a new wave of multimodal reasoning apps.

Inkling is a decoder-only multimodal Mixture-of-Experts (MoEs) model with 975B total and 41B active parameters. There are a lot of things going on, so let’s break each part down:

Here’s a quick glance of the architecture.

Relative attention: Instead of RoPE, which is the usual method to inject positional information in transformers models, Inkling uses relative attention to encode position information. Each attention layer learns position directly in the attention logits. Aside from key-query-values, there's a fourth projection producing a per-token, per-head relative feature R. This projection tensor is then tweaked with distance information (distance between the key and the query vector) and propagated into the attention module.

Hybrid attention: The decoder layers alternate between global attention (attending to the full context length at once) and sliding window attention (attending to a fixed context window in a sliding fashion). The architecture has a pattern of 5:1 sliding window to global attention layers. This hybrid attention scheme provides efficiency in computation. The final layer uses global attention to help build feature-rich representations.

Short convolution: The model uses a distinctive short 1D convolution, or SConv over the hidden states. SConv reads the current token and the previous W-1 hidden states, with W being the sliding window size. The intuition here is that SConv helps with local attention while freeing the attention and MoE modules from local representations.

MoE with shared experts sink: In Inkling, the router scores both routed experts and shared experts. Top-k selection is performed over 6 experts, plus 2 shared experts always active.

Vision understanding: The model includes a simple hierarchical MLP patchifier consisting of several linear layers. Each layer merges pixels progressively, until the final layer produces one embedding per patch.

Audio understanding: The architecture employs a discretized mel spectrogram, where each of the audio chunks (of 100 ms) are converted to the mel scale and then classified into the exact mel spectrogram bin.

The multimodal towers are relatively simple modules, unlike other models that employ separate encoders for each modality. Each image patch passes through the image embedding tower and the audio chunk is passed through the audio embedding tower to get both media embeddings. Image inputs also include an additional temporal dimension for video processing. We expect this capability to be useful for downstream fine-tuning, but we haven’t evaluated out-of-the-box video performance. The tower folds the patch grid, a small local block of neighboring tokens is stacked into the channel dimension and goes through hMLP. The audio waveform is converted to mel scale, which is then classified into a discrete mel bin. These mel bin values are embedded in the audio embedding tower and the embeddings are then summed to construct the final audio input.

Inkling 2 is the next generation of the family. It takes text and image inputs (but no audio), and generates text. It keeps the core ideas of Inkling's decoder:

Almost everything around that core was redesigned, though. The layers read from the residual stream differently, attention is bounded and gated, the MoE is simpler and wider, and the vision tower is now a real vision transformer.

Let's go over the most notable changes together:

Block attention residuals: In a standard transformer, every layer adds its output to the residual stream, and the next layer reads it. Inkling 2 has no single residual stream. Instead, it groups its 48 layers into 8 blocks of 6 and keeps one sum per block:

A sublayer (attention or MLP) doesn't read one of these sums directly. It attends over depth, which means at each token position, it treats the finished block summaries plus the current partial block as a short sequence, and takes a softmax-weighted mix of them.

The query is a single learned vector per sublayer. The keys and values are the RMS-normalized block summaries at that position. So the weights differ from token to token, depending on what each block wrote there.

In other words, each sublayer learns how much to draw from each earlier stage of the network, rather than always reading the sum of everything. By the last layer, there are up to 9 sources to choose from (the embeddings, 7 finished blocks and the current partial block), and the final norm reads its input the same way. Global attention layers learn three queries, so their query, key and value projections can each draw on a different mix of blocks.

Dynamic short convolutions: The short convolutions on keys and values in the global attention layers are now dynamic. The 4 taps of each convolution are a fixed learned weight plus a per-token weight predicted from the input, shared within each key/value head. So the model can change, token by token, how much local context goes into each key and value. All short convolutions also rescale their residual sum to keep its variance stable through depth.

A leaner, wider MoE: Each layer has 384 routed experts with 8 active per token, and the shared experts are gone.

A new vision encoder: Inkling encoded images with a lightweight hierarchical MLP. Inkling 2 uses a 23-layer vision transformer based on the Perception Encoder. It has the following properties:

Several images are packed into one sequence, and each image only attends to itself.

Inkling 2 uses the same Auto classes as Inkling. Make sure to have updated transformers to run the model.

Inkling comes with day-0 transformers support and is supported in major inference engines like SGLang and vLLM.

This model is huge. The bf16 checkpoint requires 2 TB of VRAM, while the nvfp4 version requires 600 GB of VRAM. You can try the model through serverless inference routers like Inference Providers, or use ggml quants for local deployment with llama.cpp.

The easiest way to infer with transformers directly is to use the any-to-any pipeline. You can use either the 16 bit "thinkingmachines/Inkling" on Hopper or later GPUs, or the quantized NVFP4 checkpoint "thinkingmachines/Inkling-NVFP4" on Blackwell Nvidia GPUs. Make sure to have the latest version of transformers (5.14.0 was released today) (pip install -U transformers).

After initializing the pipeline, you can pass in the prompt as follows.

Going one level lower, you can use Auto classes. For inference, you can use the AutoModelForMultimodalLM class for models and AutoProcessor class for processors. For different reasoning tasks, the tokenizer takes in a reasoning_effort argument. Existing options for reasoning effort are "none", "minimal", "low", "medium", "high", "xhigh", and "max".

For multimodal inference, you can use the same classes. We provide example snippets for each different modality in the model card.

Inkling also takes in audio input. Below is an example inference snippet, which still uses the same AutoModelForMultimodalLM class.

For more realistic parallel deployment in a cluster of several nodes, please refer to the Slurm section below.

SGLang is one of the fastest deployment frameworks for Inkling at the time of release, as it includes a custom model implementation. The launch command below shards the model across 8 GPUs and serves an OpenAI-compatible API on port 30000.

Match --tp-size to your GPU count. Add --mem-fraction-static (e.g. 0.85) if you need to leave more headroom for the KV cache.

vLLM is strong for production serving. A single vllm serve command downloads the weights from the Hub, shards the model across your GPUs with tensor parallelism, and starts an OpenAI-compatible server on port 8000. You can view the vLLM Recipe for the model here to customize to your hardware.

In practice, you might need multiple nodes and a distribution tool like SLURM (see below). Key parameters are --tensor-parallel-size to the number of GPUs on your node, and use --max-model-len to cap the context window if you hit KV-cache memory limits.

You can infer with this model using several inference providers through Hugging Face. You can see all the code snippets to consume here. Below you can see how to use with the OpenAI client.

Using the “:auto” suffix routes to your preferred provider in your settings; you can also use “cheapest” or “:fastest” as well. For this release, we cover the inference costs for 2 hours within the release for everyone.

Note: audio support in Inference Providers is work in progress and will be added shortly.

You can use llama.cpp to run quantized versions of the model on limited hardware. Unsloth have quantized the model down to 1-bit precision, reducing VRAM consumption by 95% over the original model.

This starts an OpenAI-compatible server running at http://localhost:8080/v1 that you connect to in your preferred tool or clients. Heading there, you can start chatting with the model, and set it up with your favorite MCPs, pass in images or files conveniently and more!

Llama cpp also ships with a built-in UI that supports tools, mcp, and agentic workloads. Checkout Inkling running at 1-bit precision in the llama app:

Inkling GGUFs are also runnable in Unsloth Studio with dynamic 1-bit GGUFs which retain ~74.2% of top-1% accuracy whilst being 86% smaller.

Pi is a minimal coding agent harness you can use with different language models. You can use Pi with either an inference engine server endpoint, such as llama.cpp, or with Inference Providers on Hugging Face by adding this to your ~/.pi/agent/models.json after installation.

Then you can start Pi in your project directory by calling pi and you’re good to go! In this demo, we give the model a hard math reasoning problem and it uses tools in pi to solve it.

Inkling is focused on broad multimodality reasoning and low token consumption, so try it out with document processing or audio tasks.

MTP adds extra layers to the model that predict several tokens at once, not just the next one. During inference, the extra layers act as “drafters” for speculative decoding, speeding up generation without compromising performance. With MTP, you get the exact same generated outputs, multipliers in generation speed-up at small memory cost in VRAM (due to serving the drafter). Thinking Machines also provides an MTP drafter with this release.

We have prepared a small suite of reasoning questions from expert-level sources and university entrance exams. We have taken photos of the screen with watermarks in the screenshot to challenge the model. The model has solved all of them on high one, failed one in highest and medium reasoning efforts, so we provide a link to the model answers for you to check out how the model sounds and provide the number of tokens the model has taken to solve each of them. Note that we provide no system prompts in these vibe evals, and these reasoning questions should often be run with a good system prompt. The vibe eval images and results live here.

We have vibe-evaluated the model on some audio reasoning examples from BigBenchAudio and a few multilingual audio examples of GlobeAudio (Russian and Chinese multi-choice questions asking the last word in transcription). The BigBenchAudio examples we tested consist of logical statements and questions that either ask for formal fallacies (whether an argument can be logically deduced from the context given in audio) or object counting (stating multiple distinctive objects in the audio, asking for the total count of a certain one). Although this benchmark is initially made for speech-to-speech reasoning, we just want to see audio reasoning capabilities of this model. For GlobeAudio, the questions are relatively straightforward, so we ran with reasoning efforts of 0.1. We ran the first example of each language within GlobeAudio. All tests pass on all questions and efforts, except for second formal fallacy example on lowest effort, so we only provide the number of tokens spent in each question against reasoning effort. Vibe eval results and audio files live here.

If you would like to use Inkling for post-training, Thinking Machines have built tinker, a managed tool for post-training open weight models. Their cookbook includes examples for fine-tuning, distillation, and reinforcement learning.

We post trained Inkling with tinker and OpenEnv, an agentic RL environment tool. We used the ECHO algorithm that trains a model to predict the environment without a verifier, applying next-token cross-entropy loss to tokens produced by the environment, alongside the usual policy learning on agent actions. This teaches the policy an implicit world model without requiring a separate model, teacher, or additional rollouts. Check out the example.

If you’re working with Transformers Reinforcement Learning we suggest using Inkling as a teacher model in a knowledge distillation setup. For example, take advantage of Inkling’s document understanding abilities to improve the performance of a smaller (on-device) model. In this example, we use the transformer reinforcement learning library and the GOLD algorithm to distill knowledge. GOLD is handy here because it matches token logits between different tokenizers, so you can distill to any model on the hub.

Below you can find each Inkling checkpoint as well as their VRAM requirements.

To deploy Inkling on a cluster, we provide SLURM scripts serving with transformers API, as well as how to query the endpoint with different modalities. You can adapt these scripts to vLLM or SGlang by updating the commands. These scripts live here.

You can deploy an Inkling-Small NVFP4 checkpoint using Inference Endpoints. We provide a pre-tested configuration to deploy it on 8 RTX PRO 6000s with an aggregated VRAM of·768 GB, giving large space for KV cache, costs $ 22 per hourly uptime (scales to zero when unused). To deploy, run hf endpoints catalog deploy --repo thinkingmachines/Inkling-Small-NVFP4 using the Hugging Face CLI or alternatively, head to https://endpoints.huggingface.co/new/thinkingmachines/Inkling-Small-NVFP4. With this setup, you can get 140 TPS (single user inference, prepared for multi-user support with continuous batching)

Once the endpoint is up, you can query as follows.

Releasing a natively multimodal model (text, vision, and audio) open-weights is a huge step forward for the open-source AI ecosystem! Having variable and controllable thinking effort built into a MoE architecture makes Inkling a really attractive foundation for fine-tuning. Excited to test out the smaller 12B active parameter variant for local agent workflows at https://geometrydashsubzero.io

#10027. AWS got hit by an outage too. Here's why you didn't hear about it

If a service falls in the forest and nobody hears it...

My editor asked me this week "why is everything except AWS breaking?"

It's a great question! They haven't been in the headlines! In fact, as they are wont to do, AWS spokesperson Patrick Neighorn got salty to a reporter about how unreliable Downdetector is when it started showing them as impacted.

If you'll permit me a small digression, this stems from a misunderstanding of what Downdetector is for. Historically the AWS status site was so hilariously slow to reflect the lived customer experience that some jackass (me) built a rewriter that sits at stop.lying.cloud to make it a smidgen more realistic. As a result, the question people are really trying to answer when they visit Downdetector is "my app just broke; is it my crappy code or is there a global event going on?" There are mitigations for both, but they look nothing alike.

AWS view crowdsourced reports of the form "the internet is broken, must be AWS" as a stain upon their honor. In fact, it's a badge of their own success, as "the internet" and "AWS" have become inextricably linked in people's minds.

But back to my editor's question, "why didn't AWS go down?"

AWS now has 34 generally available commercial regions, of which two are currently smoking craters due to the Iran conflict. Each of these has hundreds of services that AWS offers to customers, of which a dozen or so are high quality, if I'm being characteristically uncharitable. They experience degradation in various ways, and they go largely unnoticed.

But on November 15, AWS confirmed an incident that disrupted 11 of those ~12 good services in their oldest and most important region, us-east-1.

At 3:05 AM PST, they stated that they started seeing sign-up errors, authentication issues, and connectivity issues. Five minutes later engineers were engaged. Not to be outdone, their status page swung into action after a leisurely coffee, and posted its first indication of an incident 93 minutes later. (See previous comments on stop.lying.cloud). The all-clear showed up at 6:53 AM.

Every site has downtime. Sometimes it blows up publicly, other times nobody seems to notice. Heck, AWS said in September that it had experienced permanent data loss in its two smoking craters, but after that news cycle passed I haven't heard a thing about it. I do think it's patently unreasonable to blame them for this specific problem; "acts of war" are kinda hard to predict from the corporate planning meeting.

A few things combined to help AWS out on November 15. First, it was pre-dawn Pacific time on Sunday. Most of us slept through it; my kids aren't even up that early.

Further, the services that were most impacted (IAM Identity Center) were for engineers signing in to AWS accounts, not consumers staring at an app that stopped working.

Plus, the competition sucked all the oxygen out of the room: a day-plus Microsoft 365 364 outage and a four-hour nationwide air traffic ground stop had done a great job of level-setting what kind of outage was going to get attention, and "us-east-1 being weird but the apps still work" doesn't cut it.

Downdetector – which is owned by Accenture, so it's not like AWS doesn't have a throat to choke if they want to stop picking on reporters – measures consumer screaming. Originally, it was largely Twitter semantic analytics. This isn't a bad thing! As I said, I want to know if the internet is breaking. We can sort out exactly what part later.

The November 15 outage didn't produce that kind of screaming. Ironically, the tool that AWS is complaining about in the newspaper is the reason they skated by without notice on this outage.

Counterintuitively, Downdetector reports that outages have decreased since about 2022. Instead, what we're seeing is large-scale centralization.

Our companies don't run email systems internally anymore; we outsource to large technology companies who are almost universally better at fixing and resolving large-scale issues than we will be internally. And it feels unkind to dunk on those hard-working folks for their outages; would we want them to dunk on us for ours?

("Wait, don't you own stop.lying.cloud?" "Do as I say, not as I do.")

But whether anyone notices depends upon what layer broke, and when. If my company's email system broke on Monday, and your company's email system broke on Tuesday, the story would stop at "computers suck." But when everyone's email system goes down at once, the world takes notice.

Microsoft had to tell the whole world about a bug it mostly sat on since July.  AWS hasn't had to tell anyone anything. My editor runs a tech publication that covers this stuff for a living and didn't know. You can't buy PR like this, and AWS didn't have to.

If I were AWS, I'd stop complaining about Downdetector and send it a fruit basket. ®

#10026. Accelerating development for massive Git repositories

Android’s source code is big – the Android 17 open source release has 1,084 Git repositories, 1.62 million files, and takes 300 GB for a built workspace. Additionally, in a typical Android source tree with hardware vendor code and first-party applications, the size increases by 2-3x. Traditionally, it took over 30 minutes to fetch Android Open Source Project (AOSP) source code and well over an hour to build on even highly capable developer workstations. As software development evolved over the last 2 years, modern coding harnesses and LLMs have accelerated the development of many projects. These tools are used today for Android operating system development, but the long sync and build times make them less efficient. Both human developers and agents need quick setup, parallel workspaces, and fast build-and-test iteration times.

We built Another Build File Service (ABFS) to address these bottlenecks. ABFS is a full suite of software across a Linux kernel filesystem module, user-space daemons, and server-side infrastructure. ABFS uses content-addressability across the entire stack to lazy-load and cache source code, developer workspaces, intermediate build files, and build results.

Today, we are excited to announce that ABFS is open source on GitHub.The impact of ABFS to Android is:

ABFS already powers parallel workflows for developers and agents in Android, but it is designed to scale to other massive Git-based projects.

In the Android build system, developers define build rules in Blueprint files (Android.bp), Soong compiles them into Ninja files, and Ninja executes the final build graph (see the Android build overview). Similar to the Make build tool, Ninja is timestamp-based. If a build step’s input file is newer than the existing output file, Ninja rebuilds the output file.

Analyzing the AOSP code for Android 17 shows the sheer disk footprint and file count involved in a single checkout and build.

In a typical Android tree that includes hardware-specific repositories, board support packages, first-party applications, form-factor-specific code, etc., the code size is 2–3 times the size of AOSP (over 3,000 Git repositories), compounded across multiple active SKU and legacy maintenance branches.

Building the Cuttlefish emulator target executes a build graph with 192,249 Ninja actions. While local incremental builds are fast once a tree is already built, every new workspace, branch switch, or ephemeral agent session starts cold.Even though typical developer changes touch only 1-10 different Git projects, someone building locally without any remote execution might waste up to 80 minutes on a 64-core machine repeating work their CI system already built. Even if a developer edits a core library like system/libbase, 97% of the build graph is identical to the CI build.

Sharing cached build outputs across CI and local machines is also tricky in a codebase of Android's age and rate of change. Build rules occasionally introduce hidden dependencies (such as passing an undeclared schema file inside raw compiler flags), over-declared inputs, or undeclared outputs. In timestamp-based builds, hidden dependencies silently produce stale incremental artifacts, forcing developers to wipe output directories and run clean builds.

ABFS makes building Android fast by replacing massive local source checkouts with a virtual, content-addressable filesystem (CASFS). ABFS streams files on demand only when a build actually touches them and utilizes shared build caching to help eliminate redundant downloads and compilation.

On the server side, Git-pushers continuously ingest new Git objects from Gerrit or other Git hosts into a horizontally scalable gRPC ABFS Content-Addressable Storage (CAS) Server that indexes Git content, workspace snapshots, and build step results. On the developer host, a local Least Recently Used (LRU) Cacheman daemon, Mount Daemon, and Tap utility connect user-space build tools to the kernel filesystem so checkouts and builds stream only what they need. See the full ABFS architecture on GitHub.

At the core of the client is a virtual filesystem called Content-Addressable Storage Filesystem (CASFS), a Linux kernel module that exposes Git SHA content hashes via extended attributes. When a file's hash is set, CASFS populates its metadata immediately and downloads file bytes via Cacheman only when needed:

Initial checkouts download only lightweight directory metadata prepopulated with Git hashes. CASFS uses Git's object model natively, allowing standard git and repo operations to work transparently.

CASFS can also tap build processes. Tapping records every file actually read, written, or deleted into lists called patches, which are stored alongside cached build outputs. Ninja-go replaces timestamp checks with two-phase content-addressable caching:

Ninja-go accelerates Ninja-based builds like Android and Chrome; other build systems can integrate with ABFS's caching APIs using the same model (see the two-phase caching walkthrough on GitHub).

Each mounted checkout attaches to a persistent workspace that eagerly syncs modified files, git state, and repo state through Cacheman to the ABFS CAS Server—keeping mounts synchronized across sessions or across multiple developer hosts.

Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video

The benchmarks below show the mean time of 3 Android runs on a GCE n2d-standard-64 VM with 64 vCPUs and 256 GB of RAM. The ABFS remote server was running in the same cloud network as the client.

Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video

Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video

Link to Youtube Video (visible only when JS is disabled)

Because ABFS does lazy loading and local cache deduplication, developers and their agents can now mount multiple concurrent Android workspaces on a single machine, benefit from a shared local build cache, and achieve massive scale in development time.

An agent can check out a full Android tree in under 10 seconds and perform a full build in under 10 minutes. Agent swarms are empowered to iterate, review, and test in parallel, which can lead to higher quality solutions and speed.In the demo below, an agent makes a system/libbase fix on the latest AOSP release, then 4 parallel agents simultaneously backport, build, and test the fix across 4 more AOSP releases on a single VM.

Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video

Link to Youtube Video (visible only when JS is disabled)

We released ABFS as open source because we want developers, Android partners, and any large-scale Git-based project to benefit from what we have learned and be able to scale.

While Android’s Soong/Ninja pipeline was the first acceleration target, ABFS was built to be extensible to other build systems. Content-addressable build systems like Bazel map naturally onto CASFS and there is already a proof-of-concept integration with Bazel. Chromium, the Android Common Kernel, and other Google projects are exploring ABFS compatibility.

Explore ABFS, CASFS, and Ninja-go on GitHub, and reach out to us at abfs@google.com.

For help with the Google Cloud server-side, infrastructure-as-code, and CASFS for Cloud Workstations and Kubernetes, please reach out to abfs-gcp@google.com.

We’d like to extend a special thanks to our significant contributors for their work on this project:

#10025. A Practical Guide to Browser Developer Tools for Debugging and Improving Websites

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Building a website involves more than writing HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. Developers also need to test how their code behaves in different browsers, identify layout problems, investigate JavaScript errors, and understand why certain pages take longer to load.

Browser developer tools make these tasks easier. They provide a way to inspect the code currently running in a browser without constantly changing files or guessing what might be wrong.

Whether you're developing a new website or maintaining an existing application, learning to use these tools can improve your debugging workflow and help you write more reliable code.

Let's explore some useful browser development tools and how to apply them to everyday web development tasks.

Browser developer tools, commonly called DevTools, are built-in utilities available in modern browsers such as Google Chrome, Mozilla Firefox, Microsoft Edge, and Safari.

They allow developers to examine a webpage's HTML structure, modify CSS properties, debug JavaScript, inspect network requests, and test responsive layouts.

You can usually open them by right-clicking a webpage and selecting Inspect. On Windows and Linux, the F12 key or Ctrl + Shift + I shortcut also opens DevTools in most browsers.

The following table highlights some commonly used features:

Understanding what each panel does makes it easier to select the right tool for a particular problem.

The Elements panel is one of the most frequently used features in browser DevTools.

It displays the Document Object Model (DOM), which represents the structure of the webpage currently loaded in the browser. Developers can select individual elements and examine the CSS rules affecting their appearance.

For example, imagine that a heading has more spacing than expected. Instead of immediately editing the stylesheet, inspect the heading and review its computed styles.

You might discover that the spacing comes from a margin inherited through another CSS rule or from a conflicting selector.

You can also experiment with CSS properties directly inside DevTools.

If the card appears too wide, you can temporarily change its width or padding in the Styles panel.

The browser immediately displays the result, allowing you to compare different values without repeatedly editing and saving your stylesheet.

However, these temporary changes do not automatically update your original CSS files. Once you've identified the correct solution, apply it to your project source code.

For more detailed CSS debugging techniques, developers can also read SitePoint's guide on CSS Debugging and Optimization: Browser-based Developer Tools.

JavaScript errors can prevent interactive features from working correctly. A navigation menu might stop opening, a form might fail to submit, or a button might not trigger the expected action.

The Console panel helps developers investigate these problems.

For example, consider the following JavaScript:

If the page does not contain an element with the ID submitButton, the selected value will be null. Calling addEventListener() on that value causes an error.

You can prevent this particular issue by checking whether the element exists:

The Console panel also allows developers to execute JavaScript expressions manually.

This returns the number of image elements currently present in the document.

You can use similar expressions to inspect elements, check values, and test small pieces of functionality.

Sometimes a JavaScript error is not immediately visible. A function may execute successfully but produce an unexpected result.

In such cases, the Sources panel in Chrome DevTools or the Debugger panel in Firefox can help.

A breakpoint pauses JavaScript execution at a specific line. Developers can then inspect variable values, examine the call stack, and execute the code step by step.

If the application displays an incorrect total, you can place a breakpoint inside calculateTotal().

When the function executes, the browser pauses and allows you to inspect the values of price, quantity, and total.

This is more useful than repeatedly adding console.log() statements throughout a large application.

Breakpoints are particularly helpful when debugging complex functions, asynchronous operations, and event handlers.

A webpage may contain several resources, including images, stylesheets, JavaScript files, fonts, and API requests.

If one of these resources fails to load, part of the website may stop working correctly.

The Network panel provides information about requests made by the browser.

It displays request URLs, HTTP status codes, response sizes, loading times, and other useful details.

For example, the following table explains some common HTTP responses developers may encounter:

Suppose an image is missing from a product page. Open the Network panel, reload the page, and filter the requests by images.

If the image returns a 404 response, check whether the file path is correct and whether the resource exists on the server.

The same process can help investigate failed API requests.

For example, if a frontend application requests product information from an API, the Network panel allows you to inspect the request method, response status, and returned data.

This helps developers distinguish between frontend problems and backend errors.

A website that looks correct on a desktop computer may not work properly on a smartphone.

Text can overflow, navigation menus can become difficult to use, and images may extend beyond their containers.

Browser DevTools include responsive design and device emulation features that allow developers to test different viewport sizes.

In Chrome, you can enable the device toolbar from the DevTools interface. Firefox provides a similar feature called Responsive Design Mode.

The desktop layout displays three columns, while smaller screens display one column.

You can test this behavior by changing the viewport width inside DevTools.

A useful responsive testing process includes:

Checking common mobile and tablet widths.

Testing both portrait and landscape orientations.

Checking whether navigation remains usable.

Verifying that buttons and links are easy to interact with.

Device emulation is useful during development, but it does not completely replace testing on physical devices.

A website can have correct HTML, CSS, and JavaScript but still provide a poor experience if it loads slowly or performs unnecessary work.

The Performance panel helps developers investigate browser activity over time.

It can record page interactions and provide information about scripting, rendering, painting, and other browser operations.

For example, a page might become unresponsive when a user opens a navigation menu. A performance recording can help identify whether a long-running JavaScript function is blocking the main thread.

Developers can also use tools such as Lighthouse to audit performance, accessibility, SEO, and other aspects of a webpage.

Instead of making random optimization changes, use the available measurements to identify the actual problem.

Some useful areas to investigate include:

Performance analysis should be repeated after making changes to determine whether the optimization actually improves the result.

These features are useful, but they can also introduce debugging challenges.

For example, an application might continue displaying outdated information because an old value remains stored in local storage.

The Application panel in Chrome DevTools allows developers to inspect and manage several types of browser storage.

If the application behaves unexpectedly because of stored data, inspecting local storage can help identify the problem.

Be careful when clearing storage because doing so may remove authentication sessions, saved preferences, or other application data.

Knowing individual DevTools features is useful, but developers benefit even more from using them in a consistent order.

The following workflow can make troubleshooting more efficient:

This process helps developers identify the cause of a problem before changing multiple parts of the application.

It also makes debugging easier when working with other developers because the issue can be reproduced and explained using specific observations.

Browser developer tools are essential for modern web development. They help developers inspect HTML and CSS, debug JavaScript, analyze network requests, test responsive layouts, and investigate performance issues.

The most effective approach is to select the appropriate tool for the problem instead of making changes based on assumptions.

Whether you're working on a small website or a complex web application, becoming familiar with DevTools can make your development workflow more efficient and help you build websites that are easier to maintain.

Rather than treating debugging as something that happens only after development, make it a regular part of your workflow. This allows you to identify problems earlier, verify your solutions, and deliver more reliable web experiences.

#10024. Using Fallbacks for a Robust Front-End

Anyone who has been working in web development for a while will be familiar with this now-legendary meme from xkcd. It illustrates just how fragile the technical infrastructure of a website or app can be.

That’s why it’s important to use fallbacks to build a robust front end, either to quietly and discreetly avoid the error or to communicate it to our users.

The issue of robustness is so important that it is actually one of the four principles of the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG)! So how can we provide a modern front end without excluding users who use browsers and hardware that are only partially compatible or not compatible at all?

The answer lies in implementing multiple safety nets in HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, so that we are prepared for the worst-case scenario and can provide our users with the best possible experience.

The main difference between the use of fallbacks and progressive enhancement lies in the directions in which the two approaches aim.

While progressive enhancement is about automatically making certain features available as long as they are supported (forward), fallbacks are about what happens when something is not available or accessible (backward).

For example, we can offer a shiny new CSS feature that makes interacting with our website even more enjoyable. But if this feature isn’t available in some browsers, no one will notice, because a version that’s supported by older browsers is available instead. Progressive enhancement in action!

Another example: If JavaScript cannot be loaded for a critical application, we provide a fallback that either offers basic functionality or, at the very least, displays a message explaining what the problem is.

While one doesn’t necessarily exclude the other, their approaches are quite different. My personal recommendation is to always work with progressive enhancement as a guiding principle and to consider fallbacks whenever possible.

To evaluate new features intended for production, we must first determine the extent to which a feature is supported.

Since 2023, the Interop project has been in place, in which major browser vendors collaborate to release new features for the web platform more or less simultaneously. This serves as a general overview.

Related to this is the Baseline project, which shows, for specific features, the extent to which they are supported and how long they have been available. However, it is extremely important to note that it does not track browser support for accessibility features built into the web platform!

Another important resource for checking compatibility is Can I Use. Here, you can get a quick overview of browser support for various features.

Let’s start with the foundation of the World Wide Web: HTML. Modern tech stacks place a strong emphasis on client-side rendered JavaScript, which can offer many benefits to users in more complex applications. However, there can be just as many reasons why JavaScript might fail to load, so we need a strategy to address this.

In the event of a total failure, we should redirect users to an appropriate error page where they receive information about what went wrong and what not only they, but also we, can do to prevent this in the future. If you want to know how to write error messages that actually help users rather than frustrate them, check out Amy Hupe’s amazing article.

Because this kind of error feedback is so essential, the static site generator Astro, for example, offers the ability to add custom 404 and 500 error pages. You could discuss other possible error codes with your back-end team to implement additional safeguards.

But what if we also want to make individual sections or components more robust in case JavaScript isn’t available? For this, we can use the 

If JavaScript is not available, we will still display the components, but explain in simple and clear terms that they cannot be loaded at the moment and why that is the case.

We give users the option to reload that specific component so they can resolve the issue themselves. We also offer them the option to contact us directly via email if the problem persists.

Here, you could add a pre-written text to the  tag, which could include, for example, an internal error code specific to that component in the subject line and have a corresponding body text. This way, they would only need to click the button and could send the email directly using their email program of choice. Support would then have all the necessary information to resolve the issue without needing to ask for additional details.

No matter what your use case is, this pattern can be universally adapted and extended, and ensures that it works even if everything else goes wrong.

Let’s stick with our fictional dashboard component. Say we want to use the CSS anchor() function to display the data, which is fairly new and has solid, but not great, browser support.

Since this is a feature that can include multiple attributes, we need to check whether the ones we want to use are actually available. This is exactly where the @supports CSS rule comes into play! Here, it’s recommended to use the and operator: It should only be used if all attributes are available. If not, the more robust CSS with better browser support is used.

Here’s another fictional, simplified example:

This approach also serves as documentation: Once the feature has been around for a while and is more well-established, you can look directly for the @supports rule in your code base and check whether it is still necessary, along with its fallback.

Javascript offers us the ability to make our front end even more resilient with minimal effort. To do this, we can use the if…else statement to check whether a specific feature is available. For example, if we want to use the relatively new Navigation API, we could check for it as follows:

If we use a component-based approach, where HTML, CSS, and JavaScript are all contained in a single file, we can also use the conditional ternary operator to display this component or parts of it, or do nothing at all.

Our fictional dashboard component relies on data from the back end, and it only makes sense to display it once the data has successfully reached the front end. So, for example, we could do the following:

Depending on the use case, it makes sense to display a fallback or even nothing at all. You could also define the conditions more specifically, depending on how robust you want it to be.

My experience so far at various companies has been that the topics of fallbacks and robustness haven’t played as prominent a role as they really should have.

This is surprising, because as we’ve learned, it doesn’t take much to implement various safety nets on the front end, as long as you think ahead about what (shouldn’t) happen if something goes wrong.

HTML, CSS, and JavaScript provide us with specific elements and functions to ship robust code and thus avoid upsetting our users and, in the worst case, causing them to turn away from us.

Andy Clarke shows you how to create designs that people recognize and remember in his brand-new e-book, Standout Designs for the Web. Order it today!

#10023. Model Routing Is Simple. Until It Isn’t.

Building a router into your agent sounds like an easy win. Send simple requests to cheaper models, reserve expensive ones for harder tasks, or route by specialty — Claude for code, Gemini for multimodal, and so on. A classifier or heuristic makes the call, costs go down, performance stays up. Done.

Except it’s not. Most routing systems assume that model selection is a classification problem. In our experience building routing into agentic systems, what looks like a model-selection problem quickly becomes a systems optimization problem. Three dimensions made this surprisingly hard for us.

We expected GPT-4.1 to be cheaper than Claude Sonnet 4.6. It wasn’t.

Across 417 tasks on the AppWorld Test Challenge using the same CodeAct agent, Sonnet cost $79 total ($0.19/task) while GPT-4.1 cost $155 ($0.37/task) — nearly double. On paper, this makes no sense. GPT-4.1’s token pricing is lower on both input and output, and Sonnet takes roughly three times as many reasoning steps to finish the same tasks. By sticker price alone, GPT-4.1 should win easily.

The explanation? Caching — something most routing discussions ignore entirely. Agent workloads tend to reuse large chunks of context across steps. When cache hit rates are high, effective input costs drop dramatically. Sonnet’s lower cache-read pricing meant it benefited disproportionately from this pattern, enough to overcome both its higher base pricing and its longer trajectories.

The takeaway: actual cost depends on the interaction between the model, the workload, and the serving infrastructure. A router that only looks at pricing sheets is optimizing against the wrong numbers.

A common routing strategy is to estimate how hard a task is and send harder tasks to stronger models. Intuitive, but it breaks down in two ways.

First, difficulty is often invisible at routing time. A request like "summarize this contract" looks simple, but might trigger retrieval, compliance checks, tool use, and multiple rounds of refinement before it’s done. Meanwhile, a highly technical prompt might be handled efficiently by a smaller specialized model. You often don’t know how hard a task actually is until execution is underway.

Routers aren’t solving one problem. They’re constantly juggling cost, quality, latency, compliance, and reliability all at once.

It’s tempting to think about latency purely in terms of model size — bigger models are slower, smaller ones are faster. But what the user actually experiences depends on much more than that.

Routing itself adds overhead. Infrastructure factors — which hardware a model is running on, whether the cache is warm, how busy the endpoint is — often dominate end-to-end response times. A theoretically faster model can still produce a slower experience if the serving conditions aren’t right.

Then there’s routing granularity. Routing once per task adds minimal overhead. But routing at every step — which gives you more flexibility to adapt mid-execution — means every additional decision point introduces latency and operational complexity.

A router that ignores the serving system is optimizing against the wrong reality.

These lessons shaped how we built our router. The key shift: we stopped treating routing as a classification problem and started treating it as an optimization problem. Rather than asking "which model is best for this task?", our algorithm optimizes across cost, quality, and latency simultaneously — while staying lightweight enough to avoid becoming a bottleneck itself.

The figure below shows the result on the AppWorld Test Challenge with a CodeAct agent. Each blue square is a different configuration of our router, tracing out a cost-accuracy frontier. The important thing isn't any single point — it's that the router gives you a range of operating points to choose from depending on whether you want to prioritize cost, latency, or accuracy. Configuration 1 (latency-optimized) lands at 84% accuracy for $93 and 83s — a 21% cost reduction and 9% latency reduction compared to running Opus alone, with only a 4% accuracy drop. Configuration 2 pushes cost even lower.

Notice that a standard difficulty-based router (the teal diamond) lands in a similar accuracy range but at higher cost — it doesn't explore the full tradeoff space the way an optimization-based approach can. And because the optimization itself is lightweight (roughly 6 ms and 2 kB of memory per task), the router doesn't become the bottleneck we warned about earlier.

The lesson we took away from this work is that routing isn’t really about choosing models. It’s about optimizing systems. Models are one variable — an important one, but just one among caching behavior, infrastructure state, compliance constraints, and workload patterns.

When routing works well, it’s rarely because it found the "best" model for a given task. It’s because it found the best operating point for the entire system. That’s a harder problem than classification, but it’s the one worth solving.

We’ll be sharing more about the technical details behind our approach in a follow-up post. In the meantime, if you’re building routing into your own agentic systems, we’d love to hear what tradeoffs you’re running into.

This post was influenced by numerous conversations with colleagues, whose thoughtful questions, feedback, and insights helped refine our thinking.

So I've always felt that model routing is a false proposition; it should have been part of the harness all along.

Agreed, routing should disappear into the harness and just be part of the system's execution logic. Our goal is exactly that—making model choice an intrinsic capability rather than a separate concern.

#10022. Come for the science, stay for the big iron: Supercomputer admin on why he loves the job

From the dotcom bubble to 200,00 cores of raw power

Web hosting might seem like an unlikely on-ramp to supercomputer administration, but it set Mark O'Shea on his way to running some of Australia's most powerful machines.

O'Shea is team leader for supercomputing operations and senior supercomputing systems administrator at Australia's Pawsey Supercomputing Research Centre.

Pawsey is home to Setonix, an HPE Cray EX supercomputer with more than 200,000 AMD EPYC CPU cores and hundreds of AMD Instinct MI250X accelerators. Its GPU partition ranks 87th in the November TOP500 and 37th in the Green500, which measures computational performance per watt.

"Working in web hosting wasn't much different to what I was doing a few years later with supercomputers," O'Shea tells The Register. "Datacenters are essentially several thousand computers, as are supercomputers.

"So, we essentially had the same problems," he says, especially as regards cooling and power management.

There's no single formal route into supercomputer administration in Australia, O'Shea says. He picked up the necessary skills over time.

Andrew Underwood, Dell's chief technology officer for high-performance computing and artificial intelligence across the Asia-Pacific, Japan, and China, says that lack of formal training means some supercomputer admins start in academia.

He's observed that many HPC admins emerge from the sciences, catching the computing bug during their studies. A biologist working with a massive genomics database, for example, might discover a taste for running the systems behind it.

"The biologist might decide they want to be someone working in IT helping other biologists transform their industry," Underwood says.

"One of the things I really admire about people who work in the supercomputing field is they take it so seriously," Underwood adds. "It's almost a passion, a hobby, more so than it is a job."

"They want to play that real supporting and foundational role of assisting and engaging with scientists to help them use the technology to solve the problems the world faces."

O'Shea agrees, noting that many people who get into supercomputer admin are PhD graduates who stick around their universities after they graduate. Some of them gravitate toward running the departmental computers and then wind up in supercomputing.

"There are many roles around universities allowing people to be introduced to [supercomputer administration] while still doing enterprise-style or more departmental admin for researchers and system administration," O'Shea says.

Regardless of how a supercomputer admin gets their gig, both O'Shea and Underwood say the supersysadmin community is tight knit – which may not always be a good thing.

"As an industry in supercomputing, we need to be open to people from diverse backgrounds," Underwood says, "and we need to build these frameworks like the Student Cluster Competition, conferences like eResearch and the SC Conference, where students can get educated and systems admins get exposed to continual training."

Back at Pawsey, O'Shea notes that while the supercomputer systems admin job is interesting and challenging, there's one thing that always gives Setonix's admins a kick: seeing what scientists achieve with the machine.

One early highlight, O'Shea says, was producing a detailed image of a supernova remnant, crunching through a 43 TB dataset in the process.

"It's an exciting place to be. But everyone on my team really loves it when we hear what the researchers are doing with the supercomputers. It's very motivating when the guys get to see the end results." ®

#10021. Security incident disclosure — July 2026

Earlier this week, we detected and responded to an intrusion into part of our production infrastructure. This one was different from anything we had handled before in one important way: it was driven, end to end, by an autonomous AI agent system - and we detected and dissected it largely with AI of our own.

We identified unauthorized access to a limited set of internal datasets and to several credentials used by our services. We are still completing our assessment of whether any partner or customer data was affected, and we will contact any affected parties directly as required. We have found no evidence of tampering with public, user-facing models, datasets, or Spaces, and our software supply chain (container images and published packages) was verified clean.

The intrusion started where AI platforms are uniquely exposed: the data-processing pipeline. A malicious dataset abused two code-execution paths in our dataset processing (a remote-code dataset loader and a template-injection in a dataset configuration) to run code on a processing worker. From there, the actor escalated to node-level access, harvested cloud and cluster credentials, and moved laterally into several internal clusters over a weekend.

The campaign was run by an autonomous agent framework (appearing to be built on an agentic security-research harness - used LLM still not known) executing many thousands of individual actions across a swarm of short-lived sandboxes, with self-migrating command-and-control staged on public services. This matches the "agentic attacker" scenario the industry has been forecasting.

We are working with outside cybersecurity forensic specialists to investigate the issue and review our security policies and procedures. Finally, we have also reported this incident to law enforcement agencies.

As a precaution, we recommend rotating any access tokens and reviewing recent activity on your account. If you believe you are affected, or want to report a security concern, contact us at security@huggingface.co.

We are grateful to the teams across Hugging Face who responded around the clock, and we are sorry for any disruption this caused. Security is never finished; we will keep raising the bar.

The attack was initially surfaced through AI-assisted detection. Our anomaly-detection pipeline uses LLM-based triage over security telemetry to separate real signals from the daily noise, and it was the correlation of those signals that flagged the compromise.

To understand what a swarm of tens of thousands of automated actions did, we ran LLM-driven analysis agents over the full attacker action log, comprised of more than 17,000 recorded events. This allowed us to reconstruct the timeline, extract indicators of compromise, map the credentials touched, and separate genuine impact from decoy activity. Thanks to this approach, we were able to do in hours what would usually take days, and match the adversary's speed.

The choice of models we could use for this analysis was constrained in a way we did not anticipate; we describe this below.

When we started the log analysis, we first used frontier models behind commercial APIs. This did not work: the analysis requires submitting large volumes of real attack commands, exploit payloads, and C2 artifacts, and these requests were blocked by the providers' safety guardrails, which cannot distinguish an incident responder from an attacker. We ran the forensic analysis instead on zai-org/GLM-5.2, an open-weight model, on our own infrastructure. This had a second benefit: no attacker data, and none of the credentials it referenced, left our environment.

This experience points to a gap worth planning for. We do not know which model powered the attacker's agents, whether a jailbroken hosted model or an unrestricted open-weight one; either way, the attacker was bound by no usage policy, while our own forensic work was blocked by the guardrails of the hosted models we first tried. The practical lesson for defenders: have a capable model you can run on your own infrastructure vetted and ready before an incident, both to avoid guardrail lockout and to keep attacker data and credentials from leaving your environment. This is not an argument against safety measures on hosted models, and we are sharing this feedback with the providers concerned.

Autonomous, AI-driven offensive tooling is no longer theoretical. It lowers the cost of running a broad, patient, multi-stage campaign, and it operates at machine speed. Defending an online platform now means treating the data and model surface as a first-class attack surface, and using AI on defense to keep pace. We will keep investing there, and keep sharing what we learn.

#10020. Passive 'ghost' radar can detect airborne threats without revealing its own position

Kit piggybacks off TV and mobile signals and can be neatly stuffed into an SUV

BAE Systems is developing a passive radar system it claims could track airborne threats at a fraction of the cost of conventional radar, using existing broadcasts rather than transmitting signals that could reveal its position.

The defense biz says its covert radar technology detects reflections of television, radio, and mobile network transmissions from airborne objects. That lets it monitor airspace without broadcasting its own radar signal.

Conventional active radar transmits radio waves and measures their reflections to locate objects. But broadcasting like this is the equivalent of using a powerful searchlight to see in the dark, making the radar station itself highly visible to anyone monitoring the same radio frequencies.

Passive radar is not new, but BAE says its use of commercial off-the-shelf equipment brings the cost down to as little as a tenth that of comparable active systems. The equipment is compact enough to deploy from an SUV.

BAE says it can track targets ranging from small drones to larger aircraft and provides a clear 3D air picture with data such as target speed, heading, range and altitude. This could make it suitable for law enforcement agencies and for guarding critical national infrastructure, as well as military users.

BAE pitches the system for sites such as airports, where avoiding interference with existing equipment matters. Because it doesn't transmit its own radar signal, passive radar avoids adding another broadcast to the mix.

"While people are sat at home watching TV, our new radar technology can use transmissions from those TV and radio broadcasts without disturbance to keep crucial infrastructure such as power stations and air force bases safe from drone attacks. It also provides a boost for armed forces, allowing a soldier to monitor the battlefield undetected," says BAE's product manager for Counter-Uncrewed Systems (CUxS) Chris Shepherd.

The system will undergo live trials throughout 2027 with potential law enforcement, defense, and critical infrastructure customers, BAE says.

Elsewhere at BAE Systems, the news is less rosy: The Financial Times reports that it plans to shed more than 1,000 jobs at its head office and air division in the UK. The company says the cuts will help it become more agile and meet government demands for "greater speed and efficiency" in delivering critical defense products. ®
