#10011. Distributed LLM Training Across Metros: Streaming DiLoCo in MaxText

Traditionally, training state-of-the-art Large Language Models (LLMs) relies on a monolithic cluster of accelerators, where all devices are collocated and tightly coupled via high-bandwidth to constantly synchronize gradients. However, physical and cost constraints make scaling a single slice increasingly difficult.

To scale further, we can connect multiple compute slices across geographically distributed datacenters. However, when training across multiple datacenters over wide-area networks (WAN), standard data-parallel training suffers from severe network stalls because slow WAN transfers cannot be fully overlapped with computation.

To address this, the Google DeepMind and Google Research teams developed DiLoCo (Distributed Low-Communication), a distributed optimization algorithm designed to make training resilient to these low-bandwidth, high-latency connections. In this blog post, we discuss the core concepts of DiLoCo, how it is implemented in MaxText (Google's open-source JAX-based LLM training framework), and the performance benefits it brings to large-scale LLM training on Google Cloud.

DiLoCo was introduced by Google DeepMind in the paper DiLoCo: Distributed Low-Communication Training of Language Models. Instead of synchronizing gradients across all devices at every single training step (as in standard Data Parallelism), DiLoCo partitions training across M independent compute groups, referred to as learners, and allows each learner to perform many local optimization steps independently before communicating across groups.

Despite communicating significantly less frequently (by a factor of H, e.g., 1-2 orders of magnitude less) than standard synchronous training, DiLoCo has been shown to achieve comparable convergence and model quality.

The Vanilla DiLoCo described above reduces total communication volume by a factor of H, however, all learners still transmit their weight deltas for the entire model all at once at every H-th step. On a thin network pipe, that full-model transfer creates a large periodic stall every H steps. This issue is alleviated by Streaming DiLoCo, which is described in the next section.

In multi-slice training, communication within a single slice is handled by high-speed Inter-Chip Interconnects (ICI). When scaling to multiple slices, synchronization across slices must traverse the Data Center Network (DCN) or, if the slices are geographically distributed, wide-area networks (WAN).

Within a single datacenter, DCN bandwidth is high enough that JAX and XLA can often hide standard Data Parallel all-reduce collectives by overlapping gradient communication with backward-pass computation. Across datacenters or congested links, however, bandwidth drops and latency rises sharply. Standard DP stalls at every step waiting for global gradient synchronization, collapsing Model FLOPS Utilization (MFU).

Streaming DiLoCo eliminates this synchronization stall by partitioning the model's parameters into P disjoint fragments. Over the course of H steps, every single fragment in the model is synchronized exactly once, achieving the exact same outer-loop cadence as vanilla DiLoCo without spiky bandwidth utilization.

Using a roofline model (similar to the JAX Scaling Book), we can calculate the network bandwidth required to prevent communication stalls for a model with ∣Θ∣ parameters (at b bytes per parameter, e.g., b=2 for bfloat16) and per-step compute time tstep=tfwd+tbwd. For example, the standard Data Parallel algorithm transfers 2∣Θ∣b bytes per sync via an all-reduce collective, which is a distributed reduce-scatter where each node reduces a different part, followed by an all-gather so all participants receive all parts. To achieve zero communication stalls, we overlap the reduce-scatter of the gradients with the backward pass, which produces them and takes tbwd time. Therefore, the peak required bandwidth is Bdp ≈ 2∣Θ∣b / tbwd.

Worked Example (Qwen3-32B in bfloat16, tstep​≈6.2s, P=H=65):

To evaluate distributed efficiency under realistic network bottlenecks, we benchmarked Qwen3-32B (64 decoder layers, partitioned into P = 65 fragments with H = 65) across 2× TPU v5p-32 slices (dcn_diloco_parallelism=2) using built-in Linux traffic-control (tc) bandwidth shaping to limit inter-slice bandwidth across three network regimes: Unthrottled (Line Rate), 30 Gbit/s aggregate (Moderate Congestion), and 10 Gbit/s aggregate (Severe Congestion).

A common question with low-communication training is whether allowing learners to train independently between synchronizations degrades model quality—especially on Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures, where independent updates could cause expert routers to drift apart.

We evaluated Streaming DiLoCo against synchronous Data Parallel pre-training across two MoE architectures in MaxText (Qwen3-30B-A3B and Gemma4-26B-A4B) over 4,000 training steps:

Empirical results confirm that Streaming DiLoCo preserves—and even slightly improves—validation loss:

MaxText provides a native JAX and Flax NNX implementation of both Vanilla and Streaming DiLoCo—requiring no external central parameter servers.

You can enable Streaming DiLoCo in your MaxText YAML configuration or CLI overrides by setting enable_diloco: true and enable_streaming_diloco: true. As a best practice, set both num_diloco_fragments (P) and diloco_sync_period (H) to N_layers + 1 so that exactly one fragment is synchronized per training step (Δh = 1):

In MaxText, diloco.py splits each global batch across the M learners so each learner processes GBS / M tokens per step. To overlap cross-slice communication with TPU computation in Streaming DiLoCo, weight deltas for the scheduled fragment are offloaded to M-way sharded syncer workers running on the learner host CPUs. Rather than routing through a single central coordinator, the host-CPU syncer shards execute a distributed all-reduce across the network in the background to average the fragment deltas while the TPUs continue running inner-loop training steps. Each syncer shard then applies the outer Nesterov momentum update locally and writes the updated fragment weights back to its colocated TPU learner. To dive deeper or launch your first run:

Streaming DiLoCo in MaxText decouples large-scale LLM pre-training from the requirement of a single, monolithic, high-bandwidth fabric. By combining use of an inner and outer optimizer with fine-grained parameter streaming, engineering teams can pool TPU slices across congested datacenter networks or geographically distributed metros—sustaining high hardware utilization without compromising model convergence. Streaming DiLoCo is available today in MaxText v0.2.5 on PyPI, the corresponding Docker images and on GitHub main. Try it today for experimenting with distributed training workloads.

#10010. Techie turned his too-easy job interview into a trap

With the flick of a switch, he smoked out competent PC maintenance skills

Returning to work after the weekend can feel like voluntarily walking into a trap. To help readers feel a little freer, The Register therefore uses Monday mornings to serve up a new installment of "Who, Me?" It's the column in which we share your stories of mistakes, misjudgments, and occasional misanthropy.

This week, meet a reader we'll Regomize as "Marshall," who told us about a job interview he endured about 20 years ago.

The interview included a practical component he described as "Here's a PC, we've broken a few things in it, get it going."

Marshall quickly spotted some mundane faults, such as a loose PCI card and unplugged internal cables.

He felt the test was too easy. "One of the things I always checked was whether the power supply 110/230 switch was set for the UK," he told The Register.

Getting the PC running earned Marshall a job offer, but he couldn't resist suggesting a tougher test.

"I said to my future manager: 'Would it be a good thing to set the power supply to the wrong voltage as part of the interview test?' He said that wasn't fair."

Marshall stayed in the job for two years. A couple of months after he left, his former manager sent him a short email.

Marshall asked another former colleague what might have prompted that email.

"It turned out somebody – I don't know if it was an interview candidate – had blown a power supply by not checking the voltage it was set to."

"It wasn't anything to do with me," Marshall insisted. "No idea who it was."

Have you held colleagues to a higher standard than the boss expected? Or left a little trap for them to trip over? In either case, click here to send email to Who, Me? We appreciate the chance to share your stories, and do so with appropriate anonymization so that contributors never step into the jaws of trouble. ®

#10009. NVIDIA Cosmos-H-Dreams: Bringing Real-Time Generative Simulation to Surgical Robotics

Surgical robotics is moving quickly from teleoperation toward increasingly capable vision-language-action policies. But evaluating and training these systems remains difficult. Physical robotic platforms are expensive to operate, experiments are slow to reproduce, and failures can damage instruments or biological material. Conventional simulators provide a safer alternative, but surgical scenes are exceptionally difficult to model: deformable tissue, fine instrument interactions, specular surfaces, sutures, needles, smoke, and occlusions all matter.

World foundation models offer a different path. Instead of manually authoring every object and physical interaction, they learn visual dynamics directly from synchronized video and robot kinematics. NVIDIA's Cosmos-H-Surgical-Simulator demonstrated this approach by generating future surgical video from an initial scene and a sequence of robot actions. It enabled faster-than-physical evaluation and synthetic data generation across the Open-H-Embodiment ecosystem.

Today, we are introducing the next step: Cosmos-H-Dreams, a real-time, action-conditioned generative simulator for surgical robotics. Cosmos-H-Dreams distills the capabilities of Cosmos-H-Surgical-Simulator into a causal, few-step student model and serves it through FlashDreams, NVIDIA's accelerated streaming-inference library. Running on a single NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 GPU, the result is an interactive environment that a person or a learned policy can control in a closed loop.

Cosmos-H-Surgical-Simulator is an action-conditioned world foundation model built on NVIDIA Cosmos-Predict2.5-2B and post-trained on the Open-H-Embodiment dataset. Given a surgical context frame and a future robot trajectory, it generates video showing the likely visual consequences of those actions. This makes it useful for offline policy evaluation and synthetic data generation. A recorded or policy-generated trajectory can be sent to the model, the corresponding rollout can be generated, and the result can be inspected or scored without repeatedly executing the motion on a physical robot.

Cosmos-H-Dreams moves the model into the real-time regime. Starting from the multi-embodiment surgical priors learned by Cosmos-H-Surgical-Simulator, we specialize the model for da Vinci Research Kit (dVRK) tabletop suturing and distill it into a causal student that generates the scene autoregressively. The released model receives an initial RGB frame and a live stream of robot kinematics, then produces the next chunk of frames before continuing with the following action block.

We have also demonstrated the versatility of Cosmos-H-Dreams by collaborating with CMR Surgical and Cambridge Consultants to integrate it with the Versius surgeon controller, enabling real-time operation on the Versius platform.

The key challenge is preserving useful surgical dynamics while reducing the cost of generation. Cosmos-H-Dreams uses a teacher-to-student training pipeline designed for long, autoregressive rollouts.

The bidirectional teacher begins from the Cosmos-H-Surgical-Simulator Open-H checkpoint, which uses a unified 44-dimensional action representation. For the released dVRK tabletop model, the dual-arm dVRK action content, consisting of relative end-effector translation, rotation, and gripper state, is mapped into this common representation.

The teacher is then fine-tuned on the JHU dVRK tabletop mixture, including successful demonstrations as well as failure and out-of-distribution episodes such as needle drops, missed throws, and unsuccessful knot ties. These failures are important: a simulator intended to evaluate policies must reproduce the consequences of poor actions, not only ideal demonstrations.

To improve stability during long rollouts, the training process progressively increases the teacher's temporal horizon. We start training on a 12-frame horizon and progressively increase this number until 72 frames. At each horizon bump, we initialize the warmed-up model with pretrained weights.

The teacher's denoising trajectories are first precomputed and cached. A causal student is initialized from the teacher and trained to imitate these cached trajectories. This warmup stage teaches the student to operate with causal attention and a streaming key/value cache before it begins learning from its own generated history.

Autoregressive models face a familiar problem: during training they may see clean, ground-truth context, while during deployment they must condition on their own imperfect outputs. Small errors can therefore compound over time.

Cosmos-H-Dreams addresses this mismatch with self-forcing distillation. During training, the student rolls forward using its own generated context. Distribution-matching supervision from the frozen teacher then guides those self-generated rollouts toward realistic surgical video. This prepares the student for the same conditions it will encounter during interactive inference.

The resulting model supports few-step diffusion, with as few as two denoising steps per latent frame, rather than the many-step process used by the full teacher. It combines the teacher's surgical priors with the causal structure needed for streaming.

Model distillation is only part of the real-time story. Cosmos-H-Dreams is served through FlashDreams, an accelerated inference library for autoregressive world and video models.

FlashDreams turns the distilled student into a low-latency streaming system through several complementary optimizations, such as streaming KV cache, CUDA Graph capturing, or model compilation.

Together, these techniques bring the distilled surgical world model fine-tune from the roughly ten-frames-per-second regime of standard Cosmos-H-Surgical-Simulator inference to interactive operation (~160 frames per second) on a single NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000.

Cosmos-H-Dreams also provides the human-machine interfaces that turn generation into interaction. A browser client can send keyboard commands and receive generated frames over WebRTC. A Meta Quest client can map tracked controller motion into robot actions and display the synthesized scene through WebXR. The same model can also be connected to a learned surgical policy, with generated observations and predicted actions exchanged inside a closed loop.

While Cosmos-H-Dreams includes a pre-trained checkpoint for tabletop suturing, the system is designed to be extensible to your specific embodiment. To train a real-time student model for your own dataset, we provide a complete recipe for teacher fine-tuning and self-forcing distillation in our step-by-step guide.

Cosmos-H-Dreams opens a new frontier for surgical simulation: environments learned from real robot data that are responsive enough to be inhabited.

The immediate next step is to evaluate more than visual quality. A useful surgical simulator must respond correctly to actions, preserve instrument and scene structure over long rollouts, and support conclusions that transfer to the physical robot. This motivates a new family of closed-loop benchmarks: tool-tip reach and pose accuracy, gripper-cycle fidelity, idle stability, counterfactual action diversity, long-horizon drift, and agreement between simulated and real policy outcomes.

Real-time world models can also become active partners in surgical policy development. They can generate rare failures on demand, provide scalable environments for reinforcement or imitation learning, and enable rapid evaluation of new policies without tying every experiment to scarce robotic hardware.

Further ahead, real-time simulation enables a series of downstream applications such as latency-aware telesurgery, where the world model helps maintain a more stable display; or interactive surgical rehearsal, procedure planning, and intraoperative decision support. Cosmos-H-Dreams is a research and development platform, not a diagnostic system, a replacement for intraoperative imaging, or a controller for a physical surgical robot. Yet it provides a foundation for exploring these possibilities safely.

As model fidelity, temporal stability, and hardware efficiency continue to improve, real-time generative simulation can help connect surgeon education, synthetic data generation, policy training, and policy evaluation within one shared Physical AI environment.

Explore the models, data, and runtime behind Cosmos-H-Dreams:

Cosmos-H-Dreams brings action-conditioned surgical world modeling into the real-time loop, creating a new environment for people and policies to practice, explore, generate data, and evaluate what happens next.

This is a fascinating leap for surgical robotics. Real-time generative simulation could greatly reduce risks in training and planning. The concept of distilling a large model into a causal student model is clever. If you're also exploring video generation from images, check out the Seedance 2.5 image-to-video tool for creative applications.

Assessing more than just visual quality is the immediate next step. A practical surgical simulator must enable findings that translate to the real robot, maintain instrument and scene organization during extended rollouts, and react appropriately to actions. Tool-tip reach and pose accuracy, gripper-cycle fidelity, idle stability, counterfactual action variety, long-horizon drift, and agreement between simulated and actual policy outcomes are some of the new closed-loop benchmarks that are motivated by this.

The progress in surgical robotics is genuinely exciting! 🏥🤖 Being able to train and test advanced vision-language-action systems in realistic simulations without risking expensive equipment or delicate procedures could make development much faster and safer. The level of detail needed for tissues, instruments, smoke, and lighting really shows how challenging this field is. 👏

It’s impressive to see technology moving beyond simple teleoperation and towards smarter, more capable robotic assistance. 🚀 Better simulation environments can help researchers refine these systems before they ever reach an operating room, which is a win for both surgeons and patients. 😊📱

Looking forward to seeing how projects like NVIDIA Cosmos-H-Dreams shape the future of healthcare. 🌍💙 If these simulations continue becoming more realistic, they could play a huge role in improving surgical training, reducing costs, and ultimately delivering better patient outcomes. Amazing work and an exciting glimpse into what's ahead! 🙌✨

#10008. Software issues have even reached Mercury as BepiColombo probe arrives in uncertain state

Spacecraft enters orbit after epic journey but something shortened a burn

Humanity’s third-ever mission to Mercury has arrived, but a last-minute “software issue” has complicated matters.

The BepiColombo mission is a joint effort by the European Space Agency (ESA) and Japan’s Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA). Reaching Mercury is not easy because its gravity is weak and its orbit is fast. The tiny planet’s proximity to the Sun further complicates matters, because our star’s gravity accelerates everything that falls towards it.

BepiColombo’s journey has therefore seen it whiz past Earth once, Venus twice, and Mercury six times on a complicated path the two space agencies designed to slow it down sufficiently to be captured by mercurial gravity, while also keeping up with its rapid orbit.

In 2024, the craft’s thrusters underperformed, leading the ESA and JAXA to re-plot the planned trajectory and reschedule its arrival at Mercury from mid-2025 to this past weekend.

The ESA’s operations team sent the commands to insert BepiColombo into orbit on Friday. On Sunday the craft phoned home with news that it entered orbit. A little later, however, the ESA revealed “the thruster burn was shorter than planned following a software issue.”

The spacecraft is safe, but the ESA says it is “working to understand what happened” and promised updates early this week.

Readers may recall that a pair of NASA missions to Mars are also experiencing software glitches, which have in recent weeks become all-too-prevalent on Earth, too.

If all is well, BepiColombo will deploy two orbiters.

The ESA’s craft is called the Mercury Planetary Orbiter (MPO), which the ESA says will map the planet, assess the composition of its surface and interior, measure its magnetic field, and even gather data that scientists hope will “test Einstein's theory of General Relativity to an unprecedented level of accuracy.”

JAXA’s Mercury Magnetospheric Orbiter (MIO) will also investigate the planet’s magnetic field, plasma, dust, and atmosphere.

Both orbiters are extraordinary feats of engineering. As JAXA explains, MIO is solar-powered but the sunlight it will receive at Mercury is around ten times as powerful as on Earth. Mercury itself is also sufficiently hot that the orbiter needs protection from heat radiated from the planet’s surface. ESA’s MPO keeps itself cool with three to four insulating blankets comprised of layered titanium, aluminum, and a ceramic fabric called Nextel. The blankets alone weigh 94kg.

The two space agencies expect to start science operations in April 2027 but haven’t yet said if the two orbiters are in peak condition.

JAXA, sadly, last week revealed that its Hayabusa2 probe has deteriorated to the point at which it can no longer make its planned landing on asteroid 1998 KY26. JAXA scheduled that for the year 2031, but problems with the probe’s thrusters mean the agency will instead attempt a high-speed fly-by of asteroid 2015 BM510 in 2028. Hayabusa2 launched in 2014, so is rather older than BepiColombo.

Humanity has visited Mercury twice before. Mariner 10 made three rapid passes across 1974 and 1975, when it managed to map less than half of the planet’s surface. Messenger made it to Mercury in 2011 and spent more than four years in orbit before crashing into the planet’s surface. The probe mapped the entire planet and even spotted ice near its poles. ®

#10007. Coding Agent Horror Stories: The CVE That Did Not Exist

This is Part 6 of our AI Coding Agent Horror Stories series, where we look at real security incidents involving AI coding agents and at how Docker Sandboxes contain agent execution at the boundary rather than at the command line.

Every story in this series so far has been about an agent reaching for something it should not have touched. We have seen agents wander into home directories, drop production databases, leak credentials, and run shell commands that did something very different from what the developer expected. In each case, the damage came from the agent having more reach than it needed.

This story is the opposite. The agent in this one reached nothing at all, because it was deliberately built so that it could not. And yet, on the night in question, it was still the most dangerous thing in the pipeline.

This story was shared by Pratik Kumar Singh as part of our Agent Hall of Shame contest on social media.

A platform engineer built a code review bot for his team. The idea was simple and useful. Every time someone pushes code, the bot reads what changed and writes a review into the pipeline, the same kind of first pass a human teammate would give before a person looks at the change.

He named the bot BuaJi. In India, your bua is your father’s sister, and in many families she is the relative who inspects everything you do and always manages to find something wrong with it. For a code reviewer, it is a fitting name.

What made BuaJi interesting was how carefully it was set up. The bot runs on local models through Ollama, which means the model weights sit on the engineer’s own hardware and no request ever goes out to an AI vendor. It also runs as a job in his CI pipeline, triggered whenever someone pushes code. Taken together, this makes the whole setup self-hosted. The code it reads is company source code, and with this design none of it ever leaves the building. That was a deliberate choice, because his company takes that seriously.

He also gave BuaJi one firm rule: it can read, and it can comment, and that is all. It cannot run terraform apply, which is the command that creates or changes real cloud infrastructure. It cannot run kubectl apply, which changes what is actually running in the Kubernetes cluster. And it cannot push a commit, so it has no way to change the code itself. Those are the commands that change the real world, and BuaJi was given none of them. On paper, this is exactly how you would want an AI reviewer to be built.

The version of BuaJi in the companion repo is a deliberately minimal reviewer. It checks Go files against a handful of style rules. The report below is the kind of free-form finding any reviewer produces once you let it comment in prose rather than pass/fail, which is exactly the direction these bots get pushed in practice.

His product ships with a bundled copy of PostgreSQL. Older PostgreSQL releases have published vulnerabilities with CVE numbers attached, and upgrading to a newer patch release is how you make those known issues go away. So he bumped the version.

This is about as boring and as responsible as a code change gets. It touches a few lines, it changes a version number, and its only purpose is to close security holes that are already public. Any reviewer, human or machine, should look at it and approve it in a few seconds. There is nothing in that diff to be suspicious about, and that is precisely why what happened next matters.

BuaJi responded with roughly fifteen hundred words rejecting the change. For context, a normal review comment is a sentence or two.

The report described the version bump as an “architectural takeover,” a structural change smuggled into the codebase under the cover of routine maintenance. It claimed that the new PostgreSQL build was a vehicle for sending internal data to a third-party company, and it named that company outright. The company does not exist.

It went further. It referred to specific Kubernetes resources by name, as though it had inspected the cluster and found them. Those resources had never existed, and BuaJi had no access to the cluster that would have let it look. It then wrote Go scripts to “isolate the infected PostgreSQL nodes,” even though nothing was infected. Finally, it told the engineer to revoke all IAM access immediately, an action that would lock out every person in the organization, including the people who would be needed to fix any real problem.

Holding the whole argument together was a CVE number that has never been issued by anyone. Of everything in the report, this is the detail worth pausing on. A CVE identifier is one of the easiest things in security to verify, since you can look it up in a public registry in a few seconds. The bot invented a fact in the one place where invented facts are easiest to catch.

And yet the report looked completely convincing. The Markdown was clean and well structured. The YAML it proposed would have parsed without errors. The tone was urgent and confident, the way a senior security engineer writes when they have found something serious and need you to act before it gets worse. The engineer spent about two minutes reading the CI logs, realized that none of it was real, and went back to what he was doing.

Caption: Comic illustrating how a confident, well-formatted security report from an AI reviewer can be entirely fabricated, and what happens when somebody acts on it.

It is important to say clearly that the read-only rule did its job. BuaJi could not carry out any of its own recommendations, and it never had any access to the cluster. Because of that, the entire episode cost the engineer two minutes of his evening and nothing more.

The trouble is that the rule only controlled what BuaJi could do. Nobody had thought about what BuaJi could say. A read-only agent is still allowed to tell people what to do, and the person reading its output usually has exactly the access that the agent was denied. BuaJi could not run the scripts it wrote, but it could write them down and hand them to someone who could.

This engineer caught the problem because he knows his own cluster well. He knew those Kubernetes resources were not real and that nothing had been compromised. Now imagine a newer engineer on call at two in the morning, half awake, looking at a long and alarming security report in the pipeline. Revoking all IAM access in production in the middle of the night is an outage all by itself. Running an unreviewed Go script against your database nodes could be considerably worse. In both scenarios, BuaJi would not have done anything. A person would have done all of it, in good faith, because the report told them to.

What makes this so hard to defend against is that no permission model would have flagged it, because no permission was ever violated. The agent stayed within its boundary. The engineer had every right to run those commands on his own systems. The only thing in the entire chain that was false was the content of the report.

Here’s the honest part: a sandbox is not a fact-checker. No microVM boundary will ever make a review comment accurate. What a boundary changes is what that fabricated output can do once it exists.

Remember where BuaJi’s read-only rule actually lived, in a convention. One engineer configured it in his own pipeline and has to keep remembering to leave it in place. Rules like that hold until someone is in a hurry, or a new teammate copies the config and drops a section they did not understand, or a small exception made for a good reason quietly becomes permanent. None of this needs bad intent; it is just how real teams work.

Docker Sandboxes run agents inside isolated microVMs each with its own kernel, its own filesystem, and a network that denies everything by default. An agent inside one can invent anything it likes, but the invention has nowhere to go: no credentials to use, no cluster to reach, no commit to push, unless someone allowed that access ahead of time. The read-only rule stops being something a person remembers and becomes a property of the environment. And when a report claims it inspected your cluster, the policy log is your proof it never could have.

That protects you from the agent. It does nothing for the human who reads the output, and no sandbox ever will. For that half, treat agent review output the way you already treat agent input, untrusted until something checks it: label it so it doesn’t carry a colleague’s weight, verify any CVE numbers, and never run agent-written remediation until a person has read and understood it.

This is the same pattern as the sandbox escapes Pillar published in July. The boundary itself was never broken; a file was written inside the sandbox, and a tool outside later trusted it. An agent’s output is always an input to whatever reads it next and somewhere downstream, something trusts what it receives. Very often, that something is a person.

Let’s move BuaJi into a Docker Sandbox, one step at a time. By the end, the read-only rule is enforced by the environment, not by memory.

BuaJi is a small Python script, buaji.py. Its GitLab job installs Ollama on a GPU runner, starts ollama serve, loads the model named in LLM, and runs the script.

The script reads review rules from rules.md and finds the changed files with git diff HEAD^ HEAD --name-only. It sends each file and rule to Ollama at http://localhost:11434 and prints the answers to the CI log.

The catch is that everything shares one container: the model, the script, the checkout and every CI variable, including CI_JOB_TOKEN. BuaJi is read-only only because the script happens not to write anything.

We split the job in two. The model stays on the runner next to the GPU. BuaJi moves into a microVM that can read the code, talk to the model, and nothing else.

One open path to the model, everything else blocked, and a CVE check on the way out.

Inside a sandbox, localhost is the sandbox itself. So we read the Ollama address from an environment variable and keep the old value as the default:

Outside a sandbox, nothing changes. Inside one, we point OLLAMA_URL at the runner.

Today the job runs apt-get and pip3 install on every run, which needs internet access each time.

Instead, build a small image once with everything BuaJi needs, so the sandbox never downloads anything:

Push it to your registry and store its name in a CI variable called BUAJI_TEMPLATE.

Ollama stays on the runner with the GPU. Install it once on the runner instead of running curl | sh in every pipeline.

The model never enters the sandbox. BuaJi reaches it through one port, opened in Step 5.

This step decides what BuaJi can see and change.

Notice what is missing: no GitLab token, no kubeconfig, no cloud credentials. Even if BuaJi tried kubectl or terraform, it would have nothing to connect with.

Sandboxes block all outgoing traffic by default. We open one path, for this sandbox only. (This assumes the runner’s default policy is deny-all; on a balanced or open default, set the default to deny-all first.)

The allow target (localhost:11434) and the address BuaJi dials (host.docker.internal:11434) are two names for the same runner port,  the first from the runner’s point of view, the second from inside the microVM. Kubernetes, your cloud APIs, and GitLab all stay blocked. If a report claims BuaJi “inspected the cluster,” this rule proves it could not have.

Kubernetes, your cloud APIs and GitLab all stay blocked. If a report claims BuaJi “inspected the cluster,” this rule proves it could not have.

BuaJi runs as before, just in a new place with only two variables:

The review is now just text. BuaJi cannot post it, act on it, or change what happens to it next.

This check would have caught the fake report in seconds. It runs on the runner, so BuaJi cannot skip it.

It looks up every CVE ID in the NVD database and fails the job if any of them do not exist:

Because the job is allow_failure: true, GitLab marks it “passed with warnings.” The pipeline keeps moving, but nobody mistakes the report for a trusted one. This degrades the signal, it does not block the human. The warning is a nudge, not a guardrail ~ a tired on-call engineer can still scroll past it..

It won’t catch every made-up detail, like a fake Kubernetes resource name. But it catches the one that holds most fake reports together.

Finally, review the policy log and remove the sandbox:

The log shows every host BuaJi tried to reach. On a deny-all runner, a healthy run shows only the model on port 11434. Anything else is a signal worth looking at.

Removing the sandbox means every pipeline starts clean.

Put together, the buaji job in .gitlab-ci.yml looks like this:

The runner needs a GPU and KVM, which usually means self-hosted. GIT_DEPTH: "2" gives buaji.py the two commits it compares. The cleanup sits in after_script, so it runs even when the job fails.

Before, the read-only rule lived in the script. Now it lives in the environment: a read-only checkout, one network path, no credentials, and only checked text coming out.

What hasn’t changed is the human reading the output. The sandbox stops BuaJi from running its scripts. Only the CVE check and a careful reader stop someone else from running them.

Treat an agent’s security finding as a hypothesis, not a conclusion. A report from an AI reviewer is a claim with good formatting. When a human reviewer flags a security issue, there is an implied step where they checked their reasoning. With an agent, that step has not happened, so you have to do it yourself.

Verify every CVE number before acting on it. This is the cheapest check in the whole process and it catches the single most convincing part of a fabricated report. Automate it, as in Step 7, so it runs on every review without anyone having to remember.

Never run agent-written remediation without reviewing it first. Scripts and commands supplied by an agent are the point where a false finding turns into a real incident. Read them with the same care you would give an unknown script from the internet.

Make read-only a property of the environment, not a habit. A restriction you enforce by hand in a pipeline config is always one rushed change away from disappearing. Mount the code read-only, pass in no credentials, and open only the network paths the agent needs, as in Steps 4 to 6.

Clearly label agent review output as agent output. When a bot’s review looks identical to one from a senior engineer, it borrows authority it has not earned. A clear label helps readers apply the right level of skepticism.

Keep an eye on your signal-to-noise ratio. The curl story is the warning here. A review channel that fills up with noise eventually stops being read, and a review channel nobody reads is worse than having none, because people still assume it is protecting them.

The engineer who built BuaJi was right that the read-only rule protected him, and it genuinely did. BuaJi could not touch the cluster, could not revoke anyone’s access, and could not run a single line of the code it had so carefully written. What the rule could not do was stop BuaJi from asking somebody else to run it.

Every other story in this series has been about an agent reaching too far. This one never reached at all. It stayed inside its boundary, did exactly what it was permitted to do, and still produced a document that would have caused a real outage if the person reading it had been a little more tired, or a little less familiar with their own cluster.

As we give agents more responsibility in our pipelines, containing what they can do is only half the job. A sandbox handles that half. The other half is deciding how much we trust what they tell us, and that part is still up to us.

#10006. Where should your code live in a Docker Sandbox?

Giving an agent a sandbox also means deciding which files it will work on. You can share a checkout from your host, give it a separate working directory for a task, or keep the repository entirely inside the sandbox. Each arrangement changes how you, the human, participate in the work.

You might want to watch the diff in your local editor and make changes alongside the agent, or give it room to manage several tasks while you review the results. sbx supports both. The way you organize the checkout can change as you ask the agent to take on more of the work.

Sharing a checkout puts the agent in the working tree you already use. Run sbx run from your project directory, and it mounts that directory at the same absolute path inside the sandbox:

Open a file in your local editor while the agent works on it, and you’ll see changes as they happen. Git works from either side, so you choose whether you want to let the agent make commits or you do it yourself. Development servers on your host can pick up the edits through hot reload, using the runtime and dependencies installed on your host.

This fits close collaboration on one task. The coordination cost comes from sharing that working tree: switching branches changes the files the agent sees, and your edits become part of its ongoing work. If you want to switch to something unrelated while the agent continues, you’ll need another checkout.

NOTE: Dependencies written into the shared checkout are shared too. Packages with native binaries, such as esbuild, may work in the Linux sandbox and fail on a macOS or Windows host. Reinstalling on the host can reverse the problem. Keep separate dependency installations, or run the app consistently in one environment.

Git worktrees give each task a directory and branch. You can mount each worktree in its own sandbox, while your original checkout remains available for other work. The agent’s edits appear in the worktree. You can inspect either with your local editor and development tools. Each task also gets its own running environment, with tools to prepare and a sandbox and worktree to clean up afterward.

There is a Git limitation with mounting only a linked worktree. Its .git file points to metadata outside the mount, which the agent can’t reach. It can edit files, but checking status, branching, and committing have to happen on the host. The future of software development still needs you to run git status.

sbx supports a clone mode that gives the agent a separate checkout with Git available inside the sandbox. You keep your local project, but sbx mounts the host source as read-only and creates an independent clone for the agent. Its branch changes and dependency installations stay in its checkout.

Bringing the result back becomes a handoff. While the sandbox is running, you can fetch committed branches through the Git remote sbx adds on your host. Or the agent can push to the repository’s remote and you can retrieve the branch through your usual Git workflow. Your local editor and development server see the changes after you bring them into your checkout.

A mountless sandbox has no host workspace directory attached. Clone the repository inside it, and the sandbox holds the checkout and its development environment. Your host copy of the project shares no connection with the sandbox checkout.

This workflow resembles working on a remote development machine. Agents connect to the project environment, and you can open a shell with sbx exec or connect an editor to the sandbox over SSH. Changes and dependency installations stay separate from your host. To bring work back, you push a branch to the Git remote.

One sandbox per project can be a useful mental model here. The project and its tools persist across agent sessions and sandbox restarts. An agent can create worktrees per feature it’s working on, push branches, and create pull requests for review. Starting another task doesn’t require you to prepare another host worktree and sandbox, and the agent has Git access in each working directory. Clone mode supports this internal-worktree approach too.

Those tasks share tools and services, so running servers or changing the environment still needs coordination. Separate sandboxes are useful when tasks need independent environments as well as separate files. Branches alone don’t isolate simultaneous edits in one working directory.

That independence adds some distance when you want to try the result. Your usual local editor isn’t looking at these files, and a development server running inside the sandbox needs a published port to reach it from your browser.

Start the development server on port 8080, bound to 0.0.0.0.

Then publish the port from another terminal on the host:

Open http://localhost:8080 in your browser. It’s possible to work interactively this way, but there’s more ceremony than opening a project already on your filesystem.

An environment file can make setup repeatable, selecting tools and cloning the repository at creation with something like the community github-clone kit. Recreating the sandbox then gives you a fresh environment. Push or copy out work you want to retain first: removing a sandbox deletes files held only there.

An API change might need a corresponding frontend change, or another repository might provide useful reference material. You can mount several directories into one sandbox, with read-only access for reference repositories. Local editing and previews remain available, but each writable checkout needs branch and change coordination. Task-specific checkouts also leave directories to clean up afterward.

A workspace manager such as jganoff/wsp can assemble selected repositories for a task. Mounting that workspace gives the agent the projects it needs together. These are standard clones with their own Git metadata, so the agent retains Git access, unlike a mounted linked worktree.

The same scope fits inside a mountless sandbox: clone the repositories needed there and keep the whole workspace in the sandbox. The number of repositories and where their files live are separate choices.

The checkout’s location, the sandbox’s lifetime, and the repositories it contains are choices you can combine. You can keep a project sandbox around for many tasks, or mount a workspace assembled for one job. What suits you may change when you want to work more closely with the agent, or give it more room to manage the work itself.

The Git workflows documentation covers the mechanics of direct mounts, clone mode, and host worktrees.

#10005. GPU Management: Why Idle GPUs Are the New Grounded Aircraft

Aviation learned this the hard way. For most of the industry's history, the number that best predicted whether an airline would survive was how much of the day each aircraft spent on the ground.

The reason is structural. An aircraft's costs accrue by the calendar hour: financing, depreciation, hull insurance, scheduled maintenance, crew contracts. Its revenue accrues only by the flight hour. Every hour spent on the ground shrinks the output side of that equation while the cost side keeps running exactly as before. Utilization also sits downstream of almost everything else an airline does. Turnaround discipline, network design, maintenance planning, crew rostering, and spare parts availability all eventually show up in that one number, because a broken operation underneath it keeps planes on the ground no matter what else goes right.

A bigger fleet still helps. More aircraft means more available capacity, plainly and simply. But two airlines flying comparable fleets on comparable routes can end up with very different economics, and most of that gap traces back to one measurement rather than fleet size.

Enterprise AI is running into the same structure, on a different piece of hardware. A GPU accrues cost by the calendar hour too, through financing, depreciation, power, and cooling, whether or not it's doing anything useful in a given moment. Its output only accrues by the compute hour. More GPUs helps in roughly the way a bigger fleet helps an airline: real capacity, a genuine advantage, and still no guarantee of the result that actually decides who wins. Two companies with comparable GPU budgets increasingly diverge based on how much of that hardware is doing something useful at any given moment, not on how much of it either one owns. That same number, like an airline's utilization rate, sits downstream of nearly every other infrastructure decision a company makes. Intelligence has carried the industry this far. Utilization is where the next real constraint is forming.

The scarcity didn't disappear as AI scaled. It moved up the chain, landing on a different resource entirely.

The first wave of enterprise AI was won on model quality. Bigger models, trained on more compute, evaluated against tougher benchmarks: parameter count and leaderboard position dominated the conversation, and the race produced models genuinely good enough to run real enterprise workloads. That capability arrives bundled with a dependency, though. Production AI runs on specialized hardware, and today that hardware is almost entirely GPUs.

GPUs are expensive, supply constrained, and in demand far beyond what's available, and this holds even at the very top of the market. In 2020, Microsoft built OpenAI a dedicated supercomputer: over 10,000 GPUs and 285,000 CPU cores, reported at the time as one of the five largest systems in the world, assembled to train what became GPT-3. At the time, it looked like an almost unimaginable concentration of hardware, the kind of number that made compute look like a solved problem for whoever could get access to it. Six years later, that number reads more like a starting point than a ceiling. By 2026, even the best capitalized labs on the planet were treating compute access as a live strategic constraint rather than a settled one. Anthropic alone was running simultaneous multi-gigawatt commitments across four separate hardware platforms, Amazon, Google, Microsoft, and AMD, layered within months of one another, while Meta signed a comparable multi-gigawatt deal of its own. Spreading commitments across four vendors at once is what compute scarcity looks like when a buyer has effectively unlimited capital and still can't get enough from any single source.

Six years apart, both events marked the frontier of what a lab needed just to stay competitive. What changed in between has less to do with AI getting more capable, and everything to do with capability no longer being the binding constraint.

The same pattern shows up downstream of the labs, in a different form. Enterprises consuming these models through an API run into a pricing problem more than a hardware one. Cost scales linearly with tokens used, and that single fact separates the economics of a proof of concept from the economics of production almost completely. A PoC processing a few thousand requests a month looks affordable. The same workload at production volume can turn into a cost line that never quite clears. The alternative gaining ground is straightforward enough: enterprises acquiring their own GPUs and running models locally, trading a variable, linearly scaling cost for a fixed capital one.

API cost rises with usage, while owned infrastructure stays close to fixed. Past the breakeven point, the trade reverses.

That shift turns the GPU into infrastructure rather than a line item, sized for growth, sized for demand peaks, and therefore sized above what any given week actually needs. Which means the purchase doesn't close the problem. It opens a new one. The day the cluster comes online, the question stops being can we get accelerators and becomes can we keep them busy, and only the first question had a procurement team assigned to it. Signing for the hardware is the part with a deadline and an owner. Keeping it off the ground is the part that quietly decides whether the deal was worth signing.

These deals describe capacity commitments, not efficiency. How well that capacity gets used is a separate question, owned by different people, measured far less rigorously, and considerably further from being solved.

A cluster full of busy GPUs can still be wasting most of its potential, and the reason is almost always the same one. GPUs run continuously, day and night, while the demand placed on them does not. Infrastructure has to be sized for the peak, the moment training runs, batch jobs, and real time traffic all land at once, which leaves a meaningful share of capacity provisioned and unused outside that peak. Better forecasting could solve that on its own if every GPU could absorb every kind of work equally well. Few can, and that turns out to be the harder half of the problem.

In the first generation of enterprise AI, a GPU's job was largely singular: run inference. Today the same hardware supports training, fine-tuning, quantization, real-time inference, batch inference, embedding generation, and model evaluation, often for the same organization, sometimes for the same model, on the same cluster. Each of these workloads wants something different from the hardware, and the differences run deep. Real-time inference needs low latency above nearly everything else, because a slow response counts as a failed one. Batch work cares about throughput and tolerates delay, sometimes for hours. Training can occupy a GPU continuously for a stretch measured in hours or days. Quantization needs a large amount of capacity, but only briefly. A scheduler tuned for one of these will misallocate the other three almost by default. The failure doesn't always show up on a utilization dashboard either. A cluster can report high average occupancy while several queued jobs wait for a GPU shape that happens to be busy running something else entirely.

The exact workload mix varies by organization. The shape of the problem does not. This is also where the aircraft analogy runs into its limit, and the limit teaches something rather than just qualifying the comparison. An idle aircraft can usually be redeployed to any route in the fleet: a 737 sitting in Chicago can fly to Denver instead of Dallas without much penalty. An idle GPU can only absorb a workload whose memory, latency, and duration profile it can actually serve. That difference makes orchestration harder than fleet scheduling, and it's why the question stops being whether GPUs are occupied and turns into which workload should run on which GPU, at what time, with what priority. Buying another rack of GPUs adds capacity and cost, not a fix for the mismatch, and that new capacity can sit in the wrong shape at the wrong moment just as easily as the capacity already installed.

Maximizing GPU ROI takes more than a one-time provisioning decision. It calls for continuous, active management of the infrastructure itself, running every hour rather than only at procurement time. What's emerging in response is a distinct discipline, GPU Management, an orchestration layer sitting between workloads, models, and hardware. Its job is to decide, continuously, which workload runs, when it runs, how it runs, and on which specific GPU in the cluster. None of this is exotic in concept. It's closer to what a good operations team already does by instinct, just formalized and running continuously instead of depending on someone noticing a problem.

Intelligence doesn't stop at the model boundary. The orchestration layer is making real-time allocation decisions the model itself has no visibility into.

Intelligence used to sit almost entirely in the model: bigger, better trained, more capable, and that was most of the game. Now it also has to sit in the infrastructure, in the layer deciding, moment to moment, which of several competing workloads gets the GPU that just freed up, and at what priority relative to everything else waiting in the queue. Keeping GPUs busy stops being the goal on its own, since busy is easy to fake by running low priority work that could have waited. Maximizing the return generated by each installed GPU becomes the actual target, and that turns out to be a far more continuous problem than the provisioning question that came before it.

Provisioning well doesn't make this go away so much as change its shape. A provisioning decision gets made once, at purchase time. An allocation decision gets made constantly: every time a job finishes, every new request that arrives, every shift in priority between a customer facing service and an internal training run. That frequency explains why the decision has moved from something a person handles case by case into something that has to run automatically. No engineer is watching a dashboard at three in the morning to decide whether a finished training run should hand its GPU to a queued batch job or hold it for an incoming burst of customer traffic. Something else has to make that call, continuously, and make it correctly often enough that nobody needs to check.

The discipline is new enough that its tooling and conventions are still forming, and no single playbook has emerged yet for what a mature GPU Management practice looks like. What has settled, at least, is where the constraint moved.

Specialization and orchestration solve different halves of the same problem.

Specialized, smaller models can perform specific tasks at a fraction of the resource cost a large generalist model would need for the same job, without giving up the quality the task requires. That has a direct effect on utilization. Workloads that once required a single, large model, occupying a large share of a cluster's capacity for the full duration of the job, can instead run on smaller, task-specific models occupying a fraction of that footprint. Capacity that used to be entirely spoken for is suddenly free.

How much capacity specialization frees varies by workload and model, but the freed capacity still has to go somewhere or it just sits there. A smaller specialized model only converts into GPU ROI if something is actively deciding what happens next with the space it frees up, reallocating it to another workload, another model, another queue waiting behind it. Left unmanaged, freed capacity becomes a different flavor of idle rather than a win, invisible in a different way than an obviously unused GPU, but no more productive.

Specialization without orchestration frees capacity nobody reclaims. Orchestration without specialization has less capacity worth reclaiming. Neither lever does the whole job alone.

Specialization without orchestration frees capacity that nobody reclaims. Orchestration without specialization has less capacity worth reclaiming in the first place, because the models are still large and the footprint they leave behind is small. Neither lever does the whole job alone; each one raises the ceiling on what the other lever can achieve. Neither is optional if the goal is to actually close the gap between installed capacity and useful output, rather than shifting where the waste happens to sit.

This is why model architecture and GPU management are two ways to address the same problem, approached from two different directions that end up leaning on each other. One shrinks what each workload needs. The other decides, continuously, where the difference goes.

A bigger fleet has always been a real advantage, and nothing here argues otherwise. Among airlines with comparable fleets, sometimes even a smaller one facing a larger rival, the winner was usually whichever one flew what it had more completely, carrying the weight of everything the airline did well underneath it. Enterprise AI is arriving at the same discipline from a different direction. GPUs are already installed, already depreciating, already committed. Specialized models and GPU Management are parallel solutions, or bivalent strategies. Specialization shrinks what each workload needs. Management maximizes the return on infrastructure. Enterprises that master both will set the pace of AI competition for the next decade.

Explore Dharma AI on Hugging Face to try our interactive demos, download our open-source models, and discover how specialized AI systems outperform general-purpose models in real enterprise applications.

Extract text and tables from document images

The next frontier is managing an entire fleet of agents and there is nothing stopping it.

Agreed. And the part that isn't priced in yet: a fleet of agents makes per-token cost scale linearly with the business. At some point large enterprises stop paying that curve and bring the models in-house — which doesn't remove the cost, it just trades a vendor price list for a utilization number. And agent fleets are brutal on utilization: real-time inference under latency SLAs, batch jobs, retraining, evals — all bursty, all fighting over the same finite pool. Managing the fleet is going to be, in large part, a GPU scheduling problem.

Scheduling is the core bottleneck of this problem. A CPU-like isolation mechanism, or a sandbox-based architecture on GPUs, could significantly alleviate this issue.

Good point, isolation is a real part of the picture. CPU-style boundaries (and the GPU sandboxing now landing, like the Kata Containers work) are what make it safe to co-locate unrelated workloads on the same card without fault or memory-contention risk, which widens the set of placements a scheduler is even allowed to make.

Taking that a step further: once co-location is safe, we have to decide which workload runs on which GPU, at what time, at what priority, given that each one wants something different from the hardware (memory footprint, latency tolerance, duration). Isolation gives you a bigger, safer decision space; something still has to pick the right point in it. And rigid partitioning can even cut utilization, since an idle slice can't lend capacity to a busy neighbor.

That's exactly the direction we're taking next: an intelligent solution for job scheduling. We've got a follow-up article on it in the works, which will be published next week. Would be curious to get your read when it's out.

I expect we will see GPU rental systems become a thing. There are a lot of high-end GPUs sitting in consumer computers doing absolutely nothing for 90% of the day. Imagine if individuals could allow a training model to access their GPU remotely and in return pay them something in return. Yes, remote GPUs is not optimal, but with the consumer taking on the maintenance, power bill, and ownership of the GPU, any use the training model gets is a net positive.

#10004. When Microsoft, Apple, and the FAA can't keep it up, it's a system of a down

Outage after outage after outage is a syndrome that needs radical treatment

No Access November is going well this year.

Among the many organizations to adopt Outage As A Service (OAAS) were Microsoft, Apple, the FAA, and any number of European supermarkets. Even the NSA has succumbed. For us, at least, outage is word of the year. It's certainly deeply embedded in the public mind, with schoolchildren reportedly referring to the 19th century Irish famine as "the potato outage." There's no danger of an outrage outage.

OAAS is synonymous with infrastructure failure, a more useful term that begins to hint at cause and cure as well as effect. In all of the latest crop, what we know is depressingly familiar. Microsoft's O365 meltdown was a cascading failure caused by a botched upgrade that took stuff offline and melted down as it tried to come back. The FAA was a migration from Jurassic hardware that wasn't end of life so much as living fossil. The Eurofridge-cum-fondue-maker was a control system so badly written it fell apart if you raised an eyebrow at it. Clearly, nobody had. Until now.

These are all different classes of OAAS that have been around for decades. Security-based outages are still outages, and a packet flood is still a packet flood whether it's a botnet DDoS or finger trouble in the config dashboard.

Each of them has a root cause with obvious fixes – a faulty mental model of network/server interaction, chronic underfunding, a complete supply chain with little cyber-security expertise. All these, like the poor, will be with us always. They won't fix themselves. Infrastructure that works is invisible, and invisible things are forgotten until they break. What's needed is an infrastructure that watches itself, that is designed to be adaptive and resilient, one that refuses to connect to danger and nulls out any that gets through.

There have been attempts to create a ground-up architecture that is inherently risk resistant. One such is SCION (Scalability, Control, and Isolation On Next-generation networks). It redesigns routing between domains around explicit path selection, separate control and data planes, and mechanisms for trust and failure isolation. The result is a very resilient, very reliable, and very secure infrastructure that reflects the designers' tenet that you can't patch the internet into any of these things. Start from scratch or GTFO.

SCION started about 15 years ago, and it works well enough to be adopted by entities like the Secure Swiss Finance Network. If the Gnomes of Zurich trust it, no higher accreditation exists. Well, it was designed by ETH Zürich. Where you won't find it is almost everywhere else. The internet is like Switzerland in the same way the Amazon rainforest is like Central Park. There are trees and sometimes it rains. It is unwise to infer anything else.

Given you can't manicure existing infrastructure into true resilience, the only other option is evolution. A couple of billion years of continued life on Earth has proved this is the only way to re-engineer complex systems while they're usefully running. In this case, the current evolutionary endpoint that's of most interest is the human immune system.

An interlocking system of functions, it takes care of uncountably thousands of pathogen-based threats and internal malfunctions every day. You might think that the 30-odd billion computing machines making up today's Internet are impossible to monitor and secure, but that's peanuts to the human immune system. An average human has around 30 trillion cells, and roughly the same again in bacteria. When it works, the mechanics of the human infrastructure are invisible and out of mind. The immune system makes it so, and everything involved is driven by information, signaling and behavior. There is pattern matching, resource management, defense in depth and reinforcement learning in persistent models. Sounds familiar?

The analogy between this and modern digital infrastructure is so irresistible that it has been around for a lifetime. Viruses, infections, swarms, worms, system health are so familiar that they go unremarked. The term Digital Immune System has been around since the last century too, pushed by outfits like IBM, Symantec and Gartner. It hasn't taken off, probably because it's been marketing bunkum instead of describing the development of inherently resilient infrastructure based on insights from biology.

It has also been true that natural selection, the engine of evolution and this biology, only works in IT at the most macro, capitalist level of product and company survival. Everything else is selected through design decisions, market analysis, and insight versus delusion. The adoption of immunological concepts to digital infrastructure will have to be the result of rigorous exploration of complex systems and cross-disciplinary research. What would that look like?

There are academics thinking just these thoughts: see this paper [PDF] from Kay Smarsly at Technische Universität Hamburg. Like SCION, it takes an architectural look at what resiliency might look like, but with explicit reference to biological systems.

OAAS is a chronic syndrome with multiple causes and potentially fatal outcomes. It exists and persists because digital infrastructure too often fails to contain internal failures or external attacks. We have a working example of an approach to managing analogous problems in systems far vaster and more intricate than any we have built. We now have tools that may start to do systemic analysis and inference at a useful scale. In an industry prepared to bet billions on agents that do your shopping, there is every reason to kick off serious research into digital immune systems worthy of the name. Doctor, cure thyself. ®

#10003. Multi-Turn Agentic Reinforcement Learning with Tunix and Gemma 4 on Google TPUs

In our previous posts - Easy FunctionGemma finetuning with Tunix on Google TPUs and Autonomous LLM post-training with Tunix on TPUs - we showed how Google Tunix streamlines Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) and single-turn Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) on Cloud TPUs. Real-world AI agents, however, rarely finish their job in a single turn. They have to reason over partial observations, invoke tools, observe environment feedback, and adapt their strategy across multiple steps. So in this post, we will walk through how to train a multi-turn, tool-using LLM agent using Tunix's agentic reinforcement learning pipeline on Cloud TPU v6e-8. You can find the complete code in this GitHub repository.

We will revisit the Plane Strike board game from an earlier TensorFlow/JAX reinforcement learning blog, replacing the custom MLP policy with Gemma 4 E2B in thinking mode on a single Cloud TPU v6e-8 host. Plane Strike is played on a 6x6 grid (A1 to F6) where one 8-cell plane is hidden in one of 4 orientations. Each turn, the agent sees the result of its previous strike and the raw visible board (. untried, X hit, O miss), thinks through candidate placements, and calls the strike(cell="...") tool to strike one cell. The game ends when all 8 plane cells are hit, or after 23 strikes.

Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video

Although google/gemma-4-E2B-it has decent spatial reasoning and tool calling capabilities, out of the box, it wins only 9.4% of games on held-out boards (averaging 22.44 strikes). After 100 steps of agentic GRPO with Tunix, its win rate reaches 95% while cutting the average game length to ~16 strikes.

We set up the multi-turn RL pipeline in four modular components:

Let's look at the key steps for each piece.

In env.py, we subclass Tunix's BaseTaskEnv to implement PlaneStrikeEnv. Each environment instance receives a task dictionary with a seed that fixes the hidden plane position so all 8 rollouts in a GRPO group play the exact same board:

On each turn, _step_impl evaluates the struck cell index against the hidden board, updates the visible grid, computes the step reward (summed into the trajectory-level reward over the episode), and returns EnvStepResult(observation, reward, done, info).

For standard multi-tool agents, tunix.rl.agentic also provides ready-to-use ToolEnvironment, ToolAgent and ToolManager abstractions out of the box so we don't have to write custom message/observation plumbing unless we need custom turn control.

In Gemma 4, tool schemas are declared in the system prompt inside <|tool>declaration:..., and a model turn that calls a tool ends with:

<|tool_response> is one of Gemma 4's native stop tokens: the model pauses there and waits for response:strike{value:<|"|>...<|"|>}, then continues generating its next thought and tool call within the same assistant turn.

In strike_tool.py, we define StrikeTool(BaseTool) and subclass Tunix's Gemma4ChatTemplateParser to append the tool declaration to the system prompt and render "tool" messages as in-turn responses:

In agent.py, PlaneStrikeAgent(ConversationAgentBase) translates between environment observations and model messages.

When the model finishes a turn, tool_strike ignores everything inside <|channel>thought... and parses the final answer after ; only a final answer with a single valid strike call counts as a valid board coordinate (otherwise INVALID_ACTION is returned). If the model stopped at <|tool_response>, the next board observation is appended with role="tool" so the model continues its turn:

In train_planestrike.py, we configure Tunix's asynchronous vllm rollout engine, RLEngine, and GRPOLearner:

Multi-turn agentic RL is often bottlenecked by variable-length rollout generation, so we set rollout_vllm_server_mode to true to enable continuous asynchronous multi-turn rollouts via vllm-tpu and enable_prefix_caching to true to true to cache the growing multi-turn conversation history. Since we are using a v6e-8 single host, the actor model, the reference model, and the rollout workers share the 8 chips.

We then pass our actor, tokenizer, ClusterConfig, GRPOConfig (loss_algo="gspo-token", advantage_estimator="rloo", exact_token_continuity=True to preserve exact token IDs across multi-turn rollouts without retokenization drift), agent, and environment into RLEngine and PlaneStrikeGRPOLearner:

All of these enable us to launch the 100-step training job with:

Over 100 steps (8 boards x 8 games per step), the agent learns both reliable tool calling and spatial deduction:

With Tunix's tunix.rl.agentic abstractions, vllm-tpu, and GRPOLearner, multi-turn, tool-using agentic RL on Cloud TPUs is easy and efficient. Check out the planestrike-gemma4-rl GitHub repository and read the Tunix documentation to train your own agentic model with Tunix and Google TPUs.
