(dlv) break runtime/cgocall.go:771 Breakpoint 1 set at 0x419609 for runtime.cgoCheckUnknownPointer() /usr/local/go/src/runtime/cgocall.go:771 (dlv) c s 0x3427e8302290 &s.small 0x3427e8302298 C got 0x3427e8302298 p 0x3427e8302298 > [Breakpoint 1] runtime.cgoCheckUnknownPointer() /usr/local/go/src/runtime/cgocall.go:771 (hits goroutine(1):1 total:1) (PC: 0x419609) Warning: debugging optimized function 766: for { 767: var addr uintptr 768: if tp, addr = tp.next(base + span.elemsize); addr == 0 { 769: break 770: } => 771: pp := *(*unsafe.Pointer)(unsafe.Pointer(addr)) 772: if cgoIsGoPointer(pp) && !isPinned(pp) { 773: panic(cgoFormatErr(msg, abi.Pointer)) 774: } 775: } 776: return (dlv) print p unsafe.Pointer(0x3427e8302298) (dlv) print span.elemsize 16 (dlv) print unsafe.Pointer(addr) unsafe.Pointer(0x3427e8302290) (dlv) next > runtime.cgoCheckUnknownPointer() /usr/local/go/src/runtime/cgocall.go:772 (PC: 0x419611) Warning: debugging optimized function 767: var addr uintptr 768: if tp, addr = tp.next(base + span.elemsize); addr == 0 { 769: break 770: } 771: pp := *(*unsafe.Pointer)(unsafe.Pointer(addr)) => 772: if cgoIsGoPointer(pp) && !isPinned(pp) { 773: panic(cgoFormatErr(msg, abi.Pointer)) 774: } 775: } 776: return 777: } (dlv) print pp unsafe.Pointer(0x3427e831e008) (dlv) frame 4 print s.other (*int)(0x3427e831e008) *0 Basically, when cgo doesn't recognize how a pointer argument was written, it tells the runtime nothing about what the pointer refers to. In such cases, runtime expects all pointers in the base object to be pinned. Even though the code had nothing to do with s.other, even though the C code doesn't use this whatsoever, the runtime didn't have enough information to know that and panics conservatively. But also wrongly.Even parentheses obstruct the pattern matching:package main /* static void take(void *p) {} */ import "C" import "unsafe" type S struct { other *int small [8]byte } func main() { s := &S{other: new(int)} C.take(unsafe.Pointer((&s.small))) } main.go$ go tool cgo main.go $ sed -n '/^func main/,/^}/p' _obj/main.cgo1.go | sed -E 's| ?/\*line [^*]*\*/||g' | tr ';' '\n' | gofmt func main() { s := &S{other: new(int)} func() { _cgo0 := unsafe.Pointer((&s.small)) _cgoCheckPointer(_cgo0, nil) _Cfunc_take(_cgo0) }() } $ go run main.go 2>&1 | head -1 panic: runtime error: argument of cgo function has Go pointer to unpinned Go pointer This has been a problem in Go for a decade: golang/go#15318 and golang/go#18184 (both 2016, each closed as a duplicate), the gzip Write example in golang/go#28606 (2018, open), and golang/go#70274 (2024, closed as a duplicate), where wrapping the argument in parentheses is enough to cause the panic.In the first issue, maintainer Ian Lance Taylor called this "a known deficiency in the current cgo pointer checker." But the docs never tell you to take the address inside the call, and he explained why in 2016: "there is no intent that that be a permanent requirement. The intent is what you quote from the docs: the memory in question is the memory occupied by the field." By 2024 he wrote of a related case: "I don't know how to fix this except to do full type checking on the cgo input file, which is difficult as we currently expect the type checker to run on cgo output, not cgo input."Real-world projects have run into this too. Wails panicked on macOS because a buffer pointer was assigned to a variable before the C call. Envoy's Go extensions pass pointers that do break the rule, and its Go cluster specifier just makes everyone disable cgocheck.But let's pause and also look at what's going on here from a performance perspective.Making checks extremely expensive#If Go is checking every pointer in an object, what happens as we grow the number of pointers to check? Let's create three structs with increasingly larger arrays of pointers. We'll pass a field from the struct (with and without type info) to a C function.package ptrcost /* static void take(void *p) {} */ import "C" import "unsafe" type S1 struct { small [8]byte ptrs [1 << 10]*int } type S4 struct { small [8]byte ptrs [4 << 10]*int } type S16 struct { small [8]byte ptrs [16 << 10]*int } func inCall1(s *S1) { C.take(unsafe.Pointer(&s.small)) } func inCall4(s *S4) { C.take(unsafe.Pointer(&s.small)) } func inCall16(s *S16) { C.take(unsafe.Pointer(&s.small)) } func viaVar1(s *S1) { p := unsafe.Pointer(&s.small); C.take(p) } func viaVar4(s *S4) { p := unsafe.Pointer(&s.small); C.take(p) } func viaVar16(s *S16) { p := unsafe.Pointer(&s.small); C.take(p) } ptrcost.goAnd let's write a little benchmark wrapper.package ptrcost import "testing" func BenchmarkInCall1x(b *testing.B) { s := new(S1); for i := 0; i < b.N; i++ { inCall1(s) } } func BenchmarkInCall4x(b *testing.B) { s := new(S4); for i := 0; i < b.N; i++ { inCall4(s) } } func BenchmarkInCall16x(b *testing.B) { s := new(S16); for i := 0; i < b.N; i++ { inCall16(s) } } func BenchmarkViaVar1x(b *testing.B) { s := new(S1); for i := 0; i < b.N; i++ { viaVar1(s) } } func BenchmarkViaVar4x(b *testing.B) { s := new(S4); for i := 0; i < b.N; i++ { viaVar4(s) } } func BenchmarkViaVar16x(b *testing.B) { s := new(S16); for i := 0; i < b.N; i++ { viaVar16(s) } } ptrcost_test.goLet's try it out.$ go test -c -o ptr.test ptrcost.go ptrcost_test.go $ ./ptr.test -test.run '^$' -test.bench . -test.benchtime 200ms goos: linux goarch: amd64 cpu: Intel(R) Xeon(R) Platinum 8280 CPU @ 2.70GHz BenchmarkInCall1x-2 4633052 48.34 ns/op BenchmarkInCall4x-2 4899542 48.43 ns/op BenchmarkInCall16x-2 4904744 48.26 ns/op BenchmarkViaVar1x-2 45789 5241 ns/op BenchmarkViaVar4x-2 10000 22389 ns/op BenchmarkViaVar16x-2 3044 75748 ns/op PASS The cost stays constant even with an increasing number of pointers when passing with type info. But the cost grows linearly with the number of fields to check when passing without type info. Lack of type info, in the above case, incurs between 110x to about 1600x performance cost.The expense of checking objects full of pointers has been known since 2016.Checking only two levels deep#While the pointer checks are exhaustive in the array case, Go does not exhaustively check nested structures.We can demonstrate this with a program that builds a linked list of N nodes, pins some of the nodes after the head, and passes &head.next to a C function that walks the list.package main /* struct node { struct node *next; }; static long walk(void *p) { long n = 0; for (struct node *nd = *(struct node **)p; nd; nd = nd->next) n++; return n; } */ import "C" import ( "fmt" "os" "runtime" "strconv" "unsafe" ) type node struct { next *node } func main() { n, _ := strconv.Atoi(os.Args[1]) // nodes in the list pinned, _ := strconv.Atoi(os.Args[2]) // nodes pinned after the head var pinner runtime.Pinner defer pinner.Unpin() head := &node{} cur := head for i := 1; i < n; i++ { cur.next = &node{} cur = cur.next if i <= pinned { pinner.Pin(cur) } } walked := C.walk(unsafe.Pointer(&head.next)) fmt.Println("C walked", walked, "nodes") } main.go$ go build -o list main.go $ ./list 2 0 2>&1 | head -1 panic: runtime error: argument of cgo function has Go pointer to unpinned Go pointer $ ./list 2 1 C walked 1 nodes $ ./list 3 1 2>&1 | head -1 panic: runtime error: argument of cgo function has Go pointer to unpinned Go pointer $ ./list 3 2 C walked 2 nodes $ ./list 1000000 1 2>&1 | head -1 panic: runtime error: argument of cgo function has Go pointer to unpinned Go pointer $ ./list 1000000 2 C walked 999999 nodes The pointer we pass, &head.next, points at memory holding a pointer to node 2, so node 2 must be pinned. The check then scans node 2's object and finds node 3, so node 3 must be pinned too. But it doesn't go any further.In the last run, C reads 999,997 nodes that aren't pinned, which the docs forbid: "Go memory reachable from these function arguments must be pinned as long as the C code has access to it."Even cgocheck2, which the docs say does "complete checking", does not catch this:$ GOEXPERIMENT=cgocheck2 go build -o list main.go $ ./list 2 0 2>&1 | head -1 panic: runtime error: argument of cgo function has Go pointer to unpinned Go pointer $ ./list 3 1 2>&1 | head -1 panic: runtime error: argument of cgo function has Go pointer to unpinned Go pointer $ ./list 1000000 2 C walked 999999 nodes So we went from expensively exhaustive on the array of pointers example to cheap on the deeply nested pointer example.Parting thoughts#These examples are not exhaustive. Ian Lance Taylor has said he is "not aware of any comprehensive list of cases where this arises." You can likely find more edge cases by looking at the rewriteCall transformation in cgo, which only recognizes &x, &x[i], and x[i:j] written in a call to a C function, optionally inside type conversions. Searching Go issues for "Go pointer to unpinned Go pointer", or for the message's older wording, "Go pointer to Go pointer", may be another avenue.If you're passing a pointer to C, take the address right there in the call. It's probably worth writing a syntax checker to enforce this even. It's the difference between a 48ns call and a 76µs call. And when the cgocheck does pass, remember it only looked two levels deep, so pinning everything C can actually reach is still on you.

But also wrongly.Even parentheses obstruct the pattern matching:package main /* static void take(void *p) {} */ import "C" import "unsafe" type S struct { other *int small [8]byte } func main() { s := &S{other: new(int)} C.take(unsafe.Pointer((&s.small))) } main.go$ go tool cgo main.go $ sed -n '/^func main/,/^}/p' _obj/main.cgo1.go | sed -E 's| ?/\*line [^*]*\*/||g' | tr ';' '\n' | gofmt func main() { s := &S{other: new(int)} func() { _cgo0 := unsafe.Pointer((&s.small)) _cgoCheckPointer(_cgo0, nil) _Cfunc_take(_cgo0) }() } $ go run main.go 2>&1 | head -1 panic: runtime error: argument of cgo function has Go pointer to unpinned Go pointer This has been a problem in Go for a decade: golang/go#15318 and golang/go#18184 (both 2016, each closed as a duplicate), the gzip Write example in golang/go#28606 (2018, open), and golang/go#70274 (2024, closed as a duplicate), where wrapping the argument in parentheses is enough to cause the panic.In the first issue, maintainer Ian Lance Taylor called this "a known deficiency in the current cgo pointer checker." But the docs never tell you to take the address inside the call, and he explained why in 2016: "there is no intent that that be a permanent requirement. The intent is what you quote from the docs: the memory in question is the memory occupied by the field." By 2024 he wrote of a related case: "I don't know how to fix this except to do full type checking on the cgo input file, which is difficult as we currently expect the type checker to run on cgo output, not cgo input."Real-world projects have run into this too. Wails panicked on macOS because a buffer pointer was assigned to a variable before the C call. Envoy's Go extensions pass pointers that do break the rule, and its Go cluster specifier just makes everyone disable cgocheck.But let's pause and also look at what's going on here from a performance perspective.Making checks extremely expensive#If Go is checking every pointer in an object, what happens as we grow the number of pointers to check? Let's create three structs with increasingly larger arrays of pointers. We'll pass a field from the struct (with and without type info) to a C function.package ptrcost /* static void take(void *p) {} */ import "C" import "unsafe" type S1 struct { small [8]byte ptrs [1 << 10]*int } type S4 struct { small [8]byte ptrs [4 << 10]*int } type S16 struct { small [8]byte ptrs [16 << 10]*int } func inCall1(s *S1) { C.take(unsafe.Pointer(&s.small)) } func inCall4(s *S4) { C.take(unsafe.Pointer(&s.small)) } func inCall16(s *S16) { C.take(unsafe.Pointer(&s.small)) } func viaVar1(s *S1) { p := unsafe.Pointer(&s.small); C.take(p) } func viaVar4(s *S4) { p := unsafe.Pointer(&s.small); C.take(p) } func viaVar16(s *S16) { p := unsafe.Pointer(&s.small); C.take(p) } ptrcost.goAnd let's write a little benchmark wrapper.package ptrcost import "testing" func BenchmarkInCall1x(b *testing.B) { s := new(S1); for i := 0; i < b.N; i++ { inCall1(s) } } func BenchmarkInCall4x(b *testing.B) { s := new(S4); for i := 0; i < b.N; i++ { inCall4(s) } } func BenchmarkInCall16x(b *testing.B) { s := new(S16); for i := 0; i < b.N; i++ { inCall16(s) } } func BenchmarkViaVar1x(b *testing.B) { s := new(S1); for i := 0; i < b.N; i++ { viaVar1(s) } } func BenchmarkViaVar4x(b *testing.B) { s := new(S4); for i := 0; i < b.N; i++ { viaVar4(s) } } func BenchmarkViaVar16x(b *testing.B) { s := new(S16); for i := 0; i < b.N; i++ { viaVar16(s) } } ptrcost_test.goLet's try it out.$ go test -c -o ptr.test ptrcost.go ptrcost_test.go $ ./ptr.test -test.run '^$' -test.bench . -test.benchtime 200ms goos: linux goarch: amd64 cpu: Intel(R) Xeon(R) Platinum 8280 CPU @ 2.70GHz BenchmarkInCall1x-2 4633052 48.34 ns/op BenchmarkInCall4x-2 4899542 48.43 ns/op BenchmarkInCall16x-2 4904744 48.26 ns/op BenchmarkViaVar1x-2 45789 5241 ns/op BenchmarkViaVar4x-2 10000 22389 ns/op BenchmarkViaVar16x-2 3044 75748 ns/op PASS The cost stays constant even with an increasing number of pointers when passing with type info. But the cost grows linearly with the number of fields to check when passing without type info. Lack of type info, in the above case, incurs between 110x to about 1600x performance cost.The expense of checking objects full of pointers has been known since 2016.Checking only two levels deep#While the pointer checks are exhaustive in the array case, Go does not exhaustively check nested structures.We can demonstrate this with a program that builds a linked list of N nodes, pins some of the nodes after the head, and passes &head.next to a C function that walks the list.package main /* struct node { struct node *next; }; static long walk(void *p) { long n = 0; for (struct node *nd = *(struct node **)p; nd; nd = nd->next) n++; return n; } */ import "C" import ( "fmt" "os" "runtime" "strconv" "unsafe" ) type node struct { next *node } func main() { n, _ := strconv.Atoi(os.Args[1]) // nodes in the list pinned, _ := strconv.Atoi(os.Args[2]) // nodes pinned after the head var pinner runtime.Pinner defer pinner.Unpin() head := &node{} cur := head for i := 1; i < n; i++ { cur.next = &node{} cur = cur.next if i <= pinned { pinner.Pin(cur) } } walked := C.walk(unsafe.Pointer(&head.next)) fmt.Println("C walked", walked, "nodes") } main.go$ go build -o list main.go $ ./list 2 0 2>&1 | head -1 panic: runtime error: argument of cgo function has Go pointer to unpinned Go pointer $ ./list 2 1 C walked 1 nodes $ ./list 3 1 2>&1 | head -1 panic: runtime error: argument of cgo function has Go pointer to unpinned Go pointer $ ./list 3 2 C walked 2 nodes $ ./list 1000000 1 2>&1 | head -1 panic: runtime error: argument of cgo function has Go pointer to unpinned Go pointer $ ./list 1000000 2 C walked 999999 nodes The pointer we pass, &head.next, points at memory holding a pointer to node 2, so node 2 must be pinned. The check then scans node 2's object and finds node 3, so node 3 must be pinned too. But it doesn't go any further.In the last run, C reads 999,997 nodes that aren't pinned, which the docs forbid: "Go memory reachable from these function arguments must be pinned as long as the C code has access to it."Even cgocheck2, which the docs say does "complete checking", does not catch this:$ GOEXPERIMENT=cgocheck2 go build -o list main.go $ ./list 2 0 2>&1 | head -1 panic: runtime error: argument of cgo function has Go pointer to unpinned Go pointer $ ./list 3 1 2>&1 | head -1 panic: runtime error: argument of cgo function has Go pointer to unpinned Go pointer $ ./list 1000000 2 C walked 999999 nodes So we went from expensively exhaustive on the array of pointers example to cheap on the deeply nested pointer example.Parting thoughts#These examples are not exhaustive. Ian Lance Taylor has said he is "not aware of any comprehensive list of cases where this arises." You can likely find more edge cases by looking at the rewriteCall transformation in cgo, which only recognizes &x, &x[i], and x[i:j] written in a call to a C function, optionally inside type conversions. Searching Go issues for "Go pointer to unpinned Go pointer", or for the message's older wording, "Go pointer to Go pointer", may be another avenue.If you're passing a pointer to C, take the address right there in the call. It's probably worth writing a syntax checker to enforce this even. It's the difference between a 48ns call and a 76µs call. And when the cgocheck does pass, remember it only looked two levels deep, so pinning everything C can actually reach is still on you.

So we're definitely looking at the same address the whole time. This function is called when the runtime does not know the type of the memory that the pointer points to. It finds the full heap object containing the given pointer and validates that no unpinned pointers exist in the object slots. In our example, that means no unpinned pointer should exist in the whole object s, not just the field s.small.Following the execution with delve, we can see the above in action:$ go build -gcflags="all=-N -l" -o demo main.go Type 'help' for list of commands. We'll pass a field from the struct (with and without type info) to a C function.package ptrcost /* static void take(void *p) {} */ import "C" import "unsafe" type S1 struct { small [8]byte ptrs [1 << 10]*int } type S4 struct { small [8]byte ptrs [4 << 10]*int } type S16 struct { small [8]byte ptrs [16 << 10]*int } func inCall1(s *S1) { C.take(unsafe.Pointer(&s.small)) } func inCall4(s *S4) { C.take(unsafe.Pointer(&s.small)) } func inCall16(s *S16) { C.take(unsafe.Pointer(&s.small)) } func viaVar1(s *S1) { p := unsafe.Pointer(&s.small); C.take(p) } func viaVar4(s *S4) { p := unsafe.Pointer(&s.small); C.take(p) } func viaVar16(s *S16) { p := unsafe.Pointer(&s.small); C.take(p) } ptrcost.goAnd let's write a little benchmark wrapper.package ptrcost import "testing" func BenchmarkInCall1x(b *testing.B) { s := new(S1); for i := 0; i < b.N; i++ { inCall1(s) } } func BenchmarkInCall4x(b *testing.B) { s := new(S4); for i := 0; i < b.N; i++ { inCall4(s) } } func BenchmarkInCall16x(b *testing.B) { s := new(S16); for i := 0; i < b.N; i++ { inCall16(s) } } func BenchmarkViaVar1x(b *testing.B) { s := new(S1); for i := 0; i < b.N; i++ { viaVar1(s) } } func BenchmarkViaVar4x(b *testing.B) { s := new(S4); for i := 0; i < b.N; i++ { viaVar4(s) } } func BenchmarkViaVar16x(b *testing.B) { s := new(S16); for i := 0; i < b.N; i++ { viaVar16(s) } } ptrcost_test.goLet's try it out.$ go test -c -o ptr.test ptrcost.go ptrcost_test.go $ ./ptr.test -test.run '^$' -test.bench . -test.benchtime 200ms goos: linux goarch: amd64 cpu: Intel(R) Xeon(R) Platinum 8280 CPU @ 2.70GHz BenchmarkInCall1x-2 4633052 48.34 ns/op BenchmarkInCall4x-2 4899542 48.43 ns/op BenchmarkInCall16x-2 4904744 48.26 ns/op BenchmarkViaVar1x-2 45789 5241 ns/op BenchmarkViaVar4x-2 10000 22389 ns/op BenchmarkViaVar16x-2 3044 75748 ns/op PASS The cost stays constant even with an increasing number of pointers when passing with type info. But the cost grows linearly with the number of fields to check when passing without type info. Lack of type info, in the above case, incurs between 110x to about 1600x performance cost.The expense of checking objects full of pointers has been known since 2016.Checking only two levels deep#While the pointer checks are exhaustive in the array case, Go does not exhaustively check nested structures.We can demonstrate this with a program that builds a linked list of N nodes, pins some of the nodes after the head, and passes &head.next to a C function that walks the list.package main /* struct node { struct node *next; }; static long walk(void *p) { long n = 0; for (struct node *nd = *(struct node **)p; nd; nd = nd->next) n++; return n; } */ import "C" import ( "fmt" "os" "runtime" "strconv" "unsafe" ) type node struct { next *node } func main() { n, _ := strconv.Atoi(os.Args[1]) // nodes in the list pinned, _ := strconv.Atoi(os.Args[2]) // nodes pinned after the head var pinner runtime.Pinner defer pinner.Unpin() head := &node{} cur := head for i := 1; i < n; i++ { cur.next = &node{} cur = cur.next if i <= pinned { pinner.Pin(cur) } } walked := C.walk(unsafe.Pointer(&head.next)) fmt.Println("C walked", walked, "nodes") } main.go$ go build -o list main.go $ ./list 2 0 2>&1 | head -1 panic: runtime error: argument of cgo function has Go pointer to unpinned Go pointer $ ./list 2 1 C walked 1 nodes $ ./list 3 1 2>&1 | head -1 panic: runtime error: argument of cgo function has Go pointer to unpinned Go pointer $ ./list 3 2 C walked 2 nodes $ ./list 1000000 1 2>&1 | head -1 panic: runtime error: argument of cgo function has Go pointer to unpinned Go pointer $ ./list 1000000 2 C walked 999999 nodes The pointer we pass, &head.next, points at memory holding a pointer to node 2, so node 2 must be pinned. The check then scans node 2's object and finds node 3, so node 3 must be pinned too. But it doesn't go any further.In the last run, C reads 999,997 nodes that aren't pinned, which the docs forbid: "Go memory reachable from these function arguments must be pinned as long as the C code has access to it."Even cgocheck2, which the docs say does "complete checking", does not catch this:$ GOEXPERIMENT=cgocheck2 go build -o list main.go $ ./list 2 0 2>&1 | head -1 panic: runtime error: argument of cgo function has Go pointer to unpinned Go pointer $ ./list 3 1 2>&1 | head -1 panic: runtime error: argument of cgo function has Go pointer to unpinned Go pointer $ ./list 1000000 2 C walked 999999 nodes So we went from expensively exhaustive on the array of pointers example to cheap on the deeply nested pointer example.Parting thoughts#These examples are not exhaustive. Ian Lance Taylor has said he is "not aware of any comprehensive list of cases where this arises." You can likely find more edge cases by looking at the rewriteCall transformation in cgo, which only recognizes &x, &x[i], and x[i:j] written in a call to a C function, optionally inside type conversions. Searching Go issues for "Go pointer to unpinned Go pointer", or for the message's older wording, "Go pointer to Go pointer", may be another avenue.If you're passing a pointer to C, take the address right there in the call. It's probably worth writing a syntax checker to enforce this even. It's the difference between a 48ns call and a 76µs call. And when the cgocheck does pass, remember it only looked two levels deep, so pinning everything C can actually reach is still on you.

runtime.cgoCheckUnknownPointer panics. This function is called when the runtime does not know the type of the memory that the pointer points to. It finds the full heap object containing the given pointer and validates that no unpinned pointers exist in the object slots. In our example, that means no unpinned pointer should exist in the whole object s, not just the field s.small.Following the execution with delve, we can see the above in action:$ go build -gcflags="all=-N -l" -o demo main.go Type 'help' for list of commands. (dlv) break runtime/cgocall.go:771 Breakpoint 1 set at 0x419609 for runtime.cgoCheckUnknownPointer() /usr/local/go/src/runtime/cgocall.go:771 (dlv) c s 0x3427e8302290 &s.small 0x3427e8302298 C got 0x3427e8302298 p 0x3427e8302298 > [Breakpoint 1] runtime.cgoCheckUnknownPointer() /usr/local/go/src/runtime/cgocall.go:771 (hits goroutine(1):1 total:1) (PC: 0x419609) Warning: debugging optimized function 766: for { 767: var addr uintptr 768: if tp, addr = tp.next(base + span.elemsize); addr == 0 { 769: break 770: } => 771: pp := *(*unsafe.Pointer)(unsafe.Pointer(addr)) 772: if cgoIsGoPointer(pp) && !isPinned(pp) { 773: panic(cgoFormatErr(msg, abi.Pointer)) 774: } 775: } 776: return (dlv) print p unsafe.Pointer(0x3427e8302298) (dlv) print span.elemsize 16 (dlv) print unsafe.Pointer(addr) unsafe.Pointer(0x3427e8302290) (dlv) next > runtime.cgoCheckUnknownPointer() /usr/local/go/src/runtime/cgocall.go:772 (PC: 0x419611) Warning: debugging optimized function 767: var addr uintptr 768: if tp, addr = tp.next(base + span.elemsize); addr == 0 { 769: break 770: } 771: pp := *(*unsafe.Pointer)(unsafe.Pointer(addr)) => 772: if cgoIsGoPointer(pp) && !isPinned(pp) { 773: panic(cgoFormatErr(msg, abi.Pointer)) 774: } 775: } 776: return 777: } (dlv) print pp unsafe.Pointer(0x3427e831e008) (dlv) frame 4 print s.other (*int)(0x3427e831e008) *0 Basically, when cgo doesn't recognize how a pointer argument was written, it tells the runtime nothing about what the pointer refers to. In such cases, runtime expects all pointers in the base object to be pinned. Even though the code had nothing to do with s.other, even though the C code doesn't use this whatsoever, the runtime didn't have enough information to know that and panics conservatively. But also wrongly.Even parentheses obstruct the pattern matching:package main /* static void take(void *p) {} */ import "C" import "unsafe" type S struct { other *int small [8]byte } func main() { s := &S{other: new(int)} C.take(unsafe.Pointer((&s.small))) } main.go$ go tool cgo main.go $ sed -n '/^func main/,/^}/p' _obj/main.cgo1.go | sed -E 's| ?/\*line [^*]*\*/||g' | tr ';' '\n' | gofmt func main() { s := &S{other: new(int)} func() { _cgo0 := unsafe.Pointer((&s.small)) _cgoCheckPointer(_cgo0, nil) _Cfunc_take(_cgo0) }() } $ go run main.go 2>&1 | head -1 panic: runtime error: argument of cgo function has Go pointer to unpinned Go pointer This has been a problem in Go for a decade: golang/go#15318 and golang/go#18184 (both 2016, each closed as a duplicate), the gzip Write example in golang/go#28606 (2018, open), and golang/go#70274 (2024, closed as a duplicate), where wrapping the argument in parentheses is enough to cause the panic.In the first issue, maintainer Ian Lance Taylor called this "a known deficiency in the current cgo pointer checker." But the docs never tell you to take the address inside the call, and he explained why in 2016: "there is no intent that that be a permanent requirement. The intent is what you quote from the docs: the memory in question is the memory occupied by the field." By 2024 he wrote of a related case: "I don't know how to fix this except to do full type checking on the cgo input file, which is difficult as we currently expect the type checker to run on cgo output, not cgo input."Real-world projects have run into this too. Wails panicked on macOS because a buffer pointer was assigned to a variable before the C call. By 2024 he wrote of a related case: "I don't know how to fix this except to do full type checking on the cgo input file, which is difficult as we currently expect the type checker to run on cgo output, not cgo input."Real-world projects have run into this too. Wails panicked on macOS because a buffer pointer was assigned to a variable before the C call. Envoy's Go extensions pass pointers that do break the rule, and its Go cluster specifier just makes everyone disable cgocheck.But let's pause and also look at what's going on here from a performance perspective.Making checks extremely expensive#If Go is checking every pointer in an object, what happens as we grow the number of pointers to check? Let's create three structs with increasingly larger arrays of pointers. We'll pass a field from the struct (with and without type info) to a C function.package ptrcost /* static void take(void *p) {} */ import "C" import "unsafe" type S1 struct { small [8]byte ptrs [1 << 10]*int } type S4 struct { small [8]byte ptrs [4 << 10]*int } type S16 struct { small [8]byte ptrs [16 << 10]*int } func inCall1(s *S1) { C.take(unsafe.Pointer(&s.small)) } func inCall4(s *S4) { C.take(unsafe.Pointer(&s.small)) } func inCall16(s *S16) { C.take(unsafe.Pointer(&s.small)) } func viaVar1(s *S1) { p := unsafe.Pointer(&s.small); C.take(p) } func viaVar4(s *S4) { p := unsafe.Pointer(&s.small); C.take(p) } func viaVar16(s *S16) { p := unsafe.Pointer(&s.small); C.take(p) } ptrcost.goAnd let's write a little benchmark wrapper.package ptrcost import "testing" func BenchmarkInCall1x(b *testing.B) { s := new(S1); for i := 0; i < b.N; i++ { inCall1(s) } } func BenchmarkInCall4x(b *testing.B) { s := new(S4); for i := 0; i < b.N; i++ { inCall4(s) } } func BenchmarkInCall16x(b *testing.B) { s := new(S16); for i := 0; i < b.N; i++ { inCall16(s) } } func BenchmarkViaVar1x(b *testing.B) { s := new(S1); for i := 0; i < b.N; i++ { viaVar1(s) } } func BenchmarkViaVar4x(b *testing.B) { s := new(S4); for i := 0; i < b.N; i++ { viaVar4(s) } } func BenchmarkViaVar16x(b *testing.B) { s := new(S16); for i := 0; i < b.N; i++ { viaVar16(s) } } ptrcost_test.goLet's try it out.$ go test -c -o ptr.test ptrcost.go ptrcost_test.go $ ./ptr.test -test.run '^$' -test.bench . -test.benchtime 200ms goos: linux goarch: amd64 cpu: Intel(R) Xeon(R) Platinum 8280 CPU @ 2.70GHz BenchmarkInCall1x-2 4633052 48.34 ns/op BenchmarkInCall4x-2 4899542 48.43 ns/op BenchmarkInCall16x-2 4904744 48.26 ns/op BenchmarkViaVar1x-2 45789 5241 ns/op BenchmarkViaVar4x-2 10000 22389 ns/op BenchmarkViaVar16x-2 3044 75748 ns/op PASS The cost stays constant even with an increasing number of pointers when passing with type info. But the cost grows linearly with the number of fields to check when passing without type info. Lack of type info, in the above case, incurs between 110x to about 1600x performance cost.The expense of checking objects full of pointers has been known since 2016.Checking only two levels deep#While the pointer checks are exhaustive in the array case, Go does not exhaustively check nested structures.We can demonstrate this with a program that builds a linked list of N nodes, pins some of the nodes after the head, and passes &head.next to a C function that walks the list.package main /* struct node { struct node *next; }; static long walk(void *p) { long n = 0; for (struct node *nd = *(struct node **)p; nd; nd = nd->next) n++; return n; } */ import "C" import ( "fmt" "os" "runtime" "strconv" "unsafe" ) type node struct { next *node } func main() { n, _ := strconv.Atoi(os.Args[1]) // nodes in the list pinned, _ := strconv.Atoi(os.Args[2]) // nodes pinned after the head var pinner runtime.Pinner defer pinner.Unpin() head := &node{} cur := head for i := 1; i < n; i++ { cur.next = &node{} cur = cur.next if i <= pinned { pinner.Pin(cur) } } walked := C.walk(unsafe.Pointer(&head.next)) fmt.Println("C walked", walked, "nodes") } main.go$ go build -o list main.go $ ./list 2 0 2>&1 | head -1 panic: runtime error: argument of cgo function has Go pointer to unpinned Go pointer $ ./list 2 1 C walked 1 nodes $ ./list 3 1 2>&1 | head -1 panic: runtime error: argument of cgo function has Go pointer to unpinned Go pointer $ ./list 3 2 C walked 2 nodes $ ./list 1000000 1 2>&1 | head -1 panic: runtime error: argument of cgo function has Go pointer to unpinned Go pointer $ ./list 1000000 2 C walked 999999 nodes The pointer we pass, &head.next, points at memory holding a pointer to node 2, so node 2 must be pinned. The check then scans node 2's object and finds node 3, so node 3 must be pinned too. But it doesn't go any further.In the last run, C reads 999,997 nodes that aren't pinned, which the docs forbid: "Go memory reachable from these function arguments must be pinned as long as the C code has access to it."Even cgocheck2, which the docs say does "complete checking", does not catch this:$ GOEXPERIMENT=cgocheck2 go build -o list main.go $ ./list 2 0 2>&1 | head -1 panic: runtime error: argument of cgo function has Go pointer to unpinned Go pointer $ ./list 3 1 2>&1 | head -1 panic: runtime error: argument of cgo function has Go pointer to unpinned Go pointer $ ./list 1000000 2 C walked 999999 nodes So we went from expensively exhaustive on the array of pointers example to cheap on the deeply nested pointer example.Parting thoughts#These examples are not exhaustive. Ian Lance Taylor has said he is "not aware of any comprehensive list of cases where this arises." You can likely find more edge cases by looking at the rewriteCall transformation in cgo, which only recognizes &x, &x[i], and x[i:j] written in a call to a C function, optionally inside type conversions. Searching Go issues for "Go pointer to unpinned Go pointer", or for the message's older wording, "Go pointer to Go pointer", may be another avenue.If you're passing a pointer to C, take the address right there in the call. It's probably worth writing a syntax checker to enforce this even. It's the difference between a 48ns call and a 76µs call. And when the cgocheck does pass, remember it only looked two levels deep, so pinning everything C can actually reach is still on you.

Even parentheses obstruct the pattern matching:package main /* static void take(void *p) {} */ import "C" import "unsafe" type S struct { other *int small [8]byte } func main() { s := &S{other: new(int)} C.take(unsafe.Pointer((&s.small))) } main.go$ go tool cgo main.go $ sed -n '/^func main/,/^}/p' _obj/main.cgo1.go | sed -E 's| ?/\*line [^*]*\*/||g' | tr ';' '\n' | gofmt func main() { s := &S{other: new(int)} func() { _cgo0 := unsafe.Pointer((&s.small)) _cgoCheckPointer(_cgo0, nil) _Cfunc_take(_cgo0) }() } $ go run main.go 2>&1 | head -1 panic: runtime error: argument of cgo function has Go pointer to unpinned Go pointer This has been a problem in Go for a decade: golang/go#15318 and golang/go#18184 (both 2016, each closed as a duplicate), the gzip Write example in golang/go#28606 (2018, open), and golang/go#70274 (2024, closed as a duplicate), where wrapping the argument in parentheses is enough to cause the panic.In the first issue, maintainer Ian Lance Taylor called this "a known deficiency in the current cgo pointer checker." But the docs never tell you to take the address inside the call, and he explained why in 2016: "there is no intent that that be a permanent requirement. The intent is what you quote from the docs: the memory in question is the memory occupied by the field." By 2024 he wrote of a related case: "I don't know how to fix this except to do full type checking on the cgo input file, which is difficult as we currently expect the type checker to run on cgo output, not cgo input."Real-world projects have run into this too. Wails panicked on macOS because a buffer pointer was assigned to a variable before the C call. Envoy's Go extensions pass pointers that do break the rule, and its Go cluster specifier just makes everyone disable cgocheck.But let's pause and also look at what's going on here from a performance perspective.Making checks extremely expensive#If Go is checking every pointer in an object, what happens as we grow the number of pointers to check? Let's create three structs with increasingly larger arrays of pointers. Ian Lance Taylor has said he is "not aware of any comprehensive list of cases where this arises." You can likely find more edge cases by looking at the rewriteCall transformation in cgo, which only recognizes &x, &x[i], and x[i:j] written in a call to a C function, optionally inside type conversions. Searching Go issues for "Go pointer to unpinned Go pointer", or for the message's older wording, "Go pointer to Go pointer", may be another avenue.If you're passing a pointer to C, take the address right there in the call. It's probably worth writing a syntax checker to enforce this even. It's the difference between a 48ns call and a 76µs call. And when the cgocheck does pass, remember it only looked two levels deep, so pinning everything C can actually reach is still on you.

In the first issue, maintainer Ian Lance Taylor called this "a known deficiency in the current cgo pointer checker." But the docs never tell you to take the address inside the call, and he explained why in 2016: "there is no intent that that be a permanent requirement. The intent is what you quote from the docs: the memory in question is the memory occupied by the field." By 2024 he wrote of a related case: "I don't know how to fix this except to do full type checking on the cgo input file, which is difficult as we currently expect the type checker to run on cgo output, not cgo input."Real-world projects have run into this too. Wails panicked on macOS because a buffer pointer was assigned to a variable before the C call. Envoy's Go extensions pass pointers that do break the rule, and its Go cluster specifier just makes everyone disable cgocheck.But let's pause and also look at what's going on here from a performance perspective.Making checks extremely expensive#If Go is checking every pointer in an object, what happens as we grow the number of pointers to check? Let's create three structs with increasingly larger arrays of pointers. We'll pass a field from the struct (with and without type info) to a C function.package ptrcost /* static void take(void *p) {} */ import "C" import "unsafe" type S1 struct { small [8]byte ptrs [1 << 10]*int } type S4 struct { small [8]byte ptrs [4 << 10]*int } type S16 struct { small [8]byte ptrs [16 << 10]*int } func inCall1(s *S1) { C.take(unsafe.Pointer(&s.small)) } func inCall4(s *S4) { C.take(unsafe.Pointer(&s.small)) } func inCall16(s *S16) { C.take(unsafe.Pointer(&s.small)) } func viaVar1(s *S1) { p := unsafe.Pointer(&s.small); C.take(p) } func viaVar4(s *S4) { p := unsafe.Pointer(&s.small); C.take(p) } func viaVar16(s *S16) { p := unsafe.Pointer(&s.small); C.take(p) } ptrcost.goAnd let's write a little benchmark wrapper.package ptrcost import "testing" func BenchmarkInCall1x(b *testing.B) { s := new(S1); for i := 0; i < b.N; i++ { inCall1(s) } } func BenchmarkInCall4x(b *testing.B) { s := new(S4); for i := 0; i < b.N; i++ { inCall4(s) } } func BenchmarkInCall16x(b *testing.B) { s := new(S16); for i := 0; i < b.N; i++ { inCall16(s) } } func BenchmarkViaVar1x(b *testing.B) { s := new(S1); for i := 0; i < b.N; i++ { viaVar1(s) } } func BenchmarkViaVar4x(b *testing.B) { s := new(S4); for i := 0; i < b.N; i++ { viaVar4(s) } } func BenchmarkViaVar16x(b *testing.B) { s := new(S16); for i := 0; i < b.N; i++ { viaVar16(s) } } ptrcost_test.goLet's try it out.$ go test -c -o ptr.test ptrcost.go ptrcost_test.go $ ./ptr.test -test.run '^$' -test.bench . -test.benchtime 200ms goos: linux goarch: amd64 cpu: Intel(R) Xeon(R) Platinum 8280 CPU @ 2.70GHz BenchmarkInCall1x-2 4633052 48.34 ns/op BenchmarkInCall4x-2 4899542 48.43 ns/op BenchmarkInCall16x-2 4904744 48.26 ns/op BenchmarkViaVar1x-2 45789 5241 ns/op BenchmarkViaVar4x-2 10000 22389 ns/op BenchmarkViaVar16x-2 3044 75748 ns/op PASS The cost stays constant even with an increasing number of pointers when passing with type info. But the cost grows linearly with the number of fields to check when passing without type info. Lack of type info, in the above case, incurs between 110x to about 1600x performance cost.The expense of checking objects full of pointers has been known since 2016.Checking only two levels deep#While the pointer checks are exhaustive in the array case, Go does not exhaustively check nested structures.We can demonstrate this with a program that builds a linked list of N nodes, pins some of the nodes after the head, and passes &head.next to a C function that walks the list.package main /* struct node { struct node *next; }; static long walk(void *p) { long n = 0; for (struct node *nd = *(struct node **)p; nd; nd = nd->next) n++; return n; } */ import "C" import ( "fmt" "os" "runtime" "strconv" "unsafe" ) type node struct { next *node } func main() { n, _ := strconv.Atoi(os.Args[1]) // nodes in the list pinned, _ := strconv.Atoi(os.Args[2]) // nodes pinned after the head var pinner runtime.Pinner defer pinner.Unpin() head := &node{} cur := head for i := 1; i < n; i++ { cur.next = &node{} cur = cur.next if i <= pinned { pinner.Pin(cur) } } walked := C.walk(unsafe.Pointer(&head.next)) fmt.Println("C walked", walked, "nodes") } main.go$ go build -o list main.go $ ./list 2 0 2>&1 | head -1 panic: runtime error: argument of cgo function has Go pointer to unpinned Go pointer $ ./list 2 1 C walked 1 nodes $ ./list 3 1 2>&1 | head -1 panic: runtime error: argument of cgo function has Go pointer to unpinned Go pointer $ ./list 3 2 C walked 2 nodes $ ./list 1000000 1 2>&1 | head -1 panic: runtime error: argument of cgo function has Go pointer to unpinned Go pointer $ ./list 1000000 2 C walked 999999 nodes The pointer we pass, &head.next, points at memory holding a pointer to node 2, so node 2 must be pinned. The check then scans node 2's object and finds node 3, so node 3 must be pinned too. And when the cgocheck does pass, remember it only looked two levels deep, so pinning everything C can actually reach is still on you.

Lack of type info, in the above case, incurs between 110x to about 1600x performance cost.The expense of checking objects full of pointers has been known since 2016.Checking only two levels deep#While the pointer checks are exhaustive in the array case, Go does not exhaustively check nested structures.We can demonstrate this with a program that builds a linked list of N nodes, pins some of the nodes after the head, and passes &head.next to a C function that walks the list.package main /* struct node { struct node *next; }; static long walk(void *p) { long n = 0; for (struct node *nd = *(struct node **)p; nd; nd = nd->next) n++; return n; } */ import "C" import ( "fmt" "os" "runtime" "strconv" "unsafe" ) type node struct { next *node } func main() { n, _ := strconv.Atoi(os.Args[1]) // nodes in the list pinned, _ := strconv.Atoi(os.Args[2]) // nodes pinned after the head var pinner runtime.Pinner defer pinner.Unpin() head := &node{} cur := head for i := 1; i < n; i++ { cur.next = &node{} cur = cur.next if i <= pinned { pinner.Pin(cur) } } walked := C.walk(unsafe.Pointer(&head.next)) fmt.Println("C walked", walked, "nodes") } main.go$ go build -o list main.go $ ./list 2 0 2>&1 | head -1 panic: runtime error: argument of cgo function has Go pointer to unpinned Go pointer $ ./list 2 1 C walked 1 nodes $ ./list 3 1 2>&1 | head -1 panic: runtime error: argument of cgo function has Go pointer to unpinned Go pointer $ ./list 3 2 C walked 2 nodes $ ./list 1000000 1 2>&1 | head -1 panic: runtime error: argument of cgo function has Go pointer to unpinned Go pointer $ ./list 1000000 2 C walked 999999 nodes The pointer we pass, &head.next, points at memory holding a pointer to node 2, so node 2 must be pinned. The check then scans node 2's object and finds node 3, so node 3 must be pinned too. But it doesn't go any further.In the last run, C reads 999,997 nodes that aren't pinned, which the docs forbid: "Go memory reachable from these function arguments must be pinned as long as the C code has access to it."Even cgocheck2, which the docs say does "complete checking", does not catch this:$ GOEXPERIMENT=cgocheck2 go build -o list main.go $ ./list 2 0 2>&1 | head -1 panic: runtime error: argument of cgo function has Go pointer to unpinned Go pointer $ ./list 3 1 2>&1 | head -1 panic: runtime error: argument of cgo function has Go pointer to unpinned Go pointer $ ./list 1000000 2 C walked 999999 nodes So we went from expensively exhaustive on the array of pointers example to cheap on the deeply nested pointer example.Parting thoughts#These examples are not exhaustive. Ian Lance Taylor has said he is "not aware of any comprehensive list of cases where this arises." You can likely find more edge cases by looking at the rewriteCall transformation in cgo, which only recognizes &x, &x[i], and x[i:j] written in a call to a C function, optionally inside type conversions. Searching Go issues for "Go pointer to unpinned Go pointer", or for the message's older wording, "Go pointer to Go pointer", may be another avenue.If you're passing a pointer to C, take the address right there in the call. It's probably worth writing a syntax checker to enforce this even. It's the difference between a 48ns call and a 76µs call. And when the cgocheck does pass, remember it only looked two levels deep, so pinning everything C can actually reach is still on you.

We can demonstrate this with a program that builds a linked list of N nodes, pins some of the nodes after the head, and passes &head.next to a C function that walks the list.package main /* struct node { struct node *next; }; static long walk(void *p) { long n = 0; for (struct node *nd = *(struct node **)p; nd; nd = nd->next) n++; return n; } */ import "C" import ( "fmt" "os" "runtime" "strconv" "unsafe" ) type node struct { next *node } func main() { n, _ := strconv.Atoi(os.Args[1]) // nodes in the list pinned, _ := strconv.Atoi(os.Args[2]) // nodes pinned after the head var pinner runtime.Pinner defer pinner.Unpin() head := &node{} cur := head for i := 1; i < n; i++ { cur.next = &node{} cur = cur.next if i <= pinned { pinner.Pin(cur) } } walked := C.walk(unsafe.Pointer(&head.next)) fmt.Println("C walked", walked, "nodes") } main.go$ go build -o list main.go $ ./list 2 0 2>&1 | head -1 panic: runtime error: argument of cgo function has Go pointer to unpinned Go pointer $ ./list 2 1 C walked 1 nodes $ ./list 3 1 2>&1 | head -1 panic: runtime error: argument of cgo function has Go pointer to unpinned Go pointer $ ./list 3 2 C walked 2 nodes $ ./list 1000000 1 2>&1 | head -1 panic: runtime error: argument of cgo function has Go pointer to unpinned Go pointer $ ./list 1000000 2 C walked 999999 nodes The pointer we pass, &head.next, points at memory holding a pointer to node 2, so node 2 must be pinned. The check then scans node 2's object and finds node 3, so node 3 must be pinned too. But it doesn't go any further.In the last run, C reads 999,997 nodes that aren't pinned, which the docs forbid: "Go memory reachable from these function arguments must be pinned as long as the C code has access to it."Even cgocheck2, which the docs say does "complete checking", does not catch this:$ GOEXPERIMENT=cgocheck2 go build -o list main.go $ ./list 2 0 2>&1 | head -1 panic: runtime error: argument of cgo function has Go pointer to unpinned Go pointer $ ./list 3 1 2>&1 | head -1 panic: runtime error: argument of cgo function has Go pointer to unpinned Go pointer $ ./list 1000000 2 C walked 999999 nodes So we went from expensively exhaustive on the array of pointers example to cheap on the deeply nested pointer example.Parting thoughts#These examples are not exhaustive. Ian Lance Taylor has said he is "not aware of any comprehensive list of cases where this arises." You can likely find more edge cases by looking at the rewriteCall transformation in cgo, which only recognizes &x, &x[i], and x[i:j] written in a call to a C function, optionally inside type conversions. Searching Go issues for "Go pointer to unpinned Go pointer", or for the message's older wording, "Go pointer to Go pointer", may be another avenue.If you're passing a pointer to C, take the address right there in the call. It's probably worth writing a syntax checker to enforce this even. It's the difference between a 48ns call and a 76µs call. And when the cgocheck does pass, remember it only looked two levels deep, so pinning everything C can actually reach is still on you.

#9907. 9/UX brings a classic Mac feel to 9front

A spatial classic Finder in the style of A/UX

Bringing a classic MacOS Finder to Linux is all very well, but there's no shortage of Linux desktops… however, bringing one to 9front is even more unexpected – and even more useful.

9/UX is a new project by Jeff "Progrium" Lindsay, who was one of the people behind Docker, Webhooks, and more. When you follow that link, and you should, pay close attention to what looks like a screenshot at the top. It is not an image. It's a real live executing instance of the OS, running inside your web browser, running on top of hyper9. (That is worth reading too – it's an impressive project in its own right.)

As its GitHub repository describes, 9/UX is a "Macintosh-inspired graphical environment for 9front."

"9/UX brings the classic Mac and A/UX desktop experience (a spatial desktop, a global menu bar, consistent controls and dialogs, icons, and resource-driven presentation) to 9front, built the Plan 9 way: rio and libdraw draw the screen, 9P exposes every application's UI state and commands as files, namespaces define the working environment, the plumber opens documents, and ndb holds human-editable metadata."

Lindsay introduced 9/UX earlier this month in a short X thread, saying he "made my own kind of A/UX but on Plan 9." In its creator's own words, "it's slop", but this is kind of interesting, original, creative bot-assisted coding that we enjoy looking at. At the end of last week, he returned to explain more:

"9/UX isn’t just a pretty Mac-style UI on Plan 9. It's filesystem inspectable. Shell scriptable. Even the Mac resource file format can be used through the filesystem."

Regular readers may have noticed that The Reg FOSS desk is fascinated by Plan 9 and its FOSS continuation 9front. We've written and presented at length about this remarkable OS, and tried to explain its FOSS continuation 9front several times. But even with the best will we can muster, its unique GUI is not an especially friendly or easy one. Its idiosyncratic UI was inspired by the late great Niklaus Wirth's unbelievably tiny Oberon OS, which we have written about before. It's cryptic, and that's being generous.

The research and development effort that led to Unix didn't stop when Unix 7th Edition escaped from the Bell Labs in 1981 and mutated into Unix System III. The industry enthusiastically adopted System III and later System V. A decade after 7th Edition Unix, Linux became a GPL version of something very like that traditional Unix, closely followed by the BSDs – and between them, they have very effectively distracted most of the FOSS world ever since. Even so, Research Unix lived on, saw 8th, 9th, and 10th editions, and then was replaced by Plan 9. In 1996, many of Plan 9's limitations were overcome by Inferno – whose revival as InferNode we covered this week.

We always vaguely thought that if 9front were to receive an improved GUI that was slightly more compliant with later GUI design standards, it might be with a version of the Inferno UI… But apparently not. A new, easier, and yet still simple, clean and attractive desktop for 9front is here, and it looks like classic MacOS from the era of Apple's 68030 Unix A/UX.

We do not think the chances are high that the 9front community will adopt this with enthusiasm. Even so, there is an AI programming manual for agents, and we've seen some interesting looking LLM-assisted 9front apps of late. Several can be found in the agent9 distribution, which includes LLM-assisted ports of C++, Python, and Rust, plus a version of DOSbox, and even a package manager called pac9.®

#9906. Rebuilding AUTOMATIC1111 with Gradio Workflow

In our last post, we built five small gr.Workflow graphs and hinted at what it would take to build something as complex as AUTOMATIC1111's stable-diffusion-webui. In this post we walk you through Workflow1111, where we have rebuilt most of AUTOMATIC1111's feature set as a single workflow canvas.

Workflow1111 is a graph of eleven media pipelines built using seventy-three nodes. It brings together SOTA models for text-to-image, hi-resolution fix, image-to-image, prompt-matrix grids, VLM interrogate, detection-to-inpaint masks, ControlNet-style annotators, background removal, PNG Info storing, and image-to-video.

You can run any of these pipelines by signing in with your Hugging Face account or providing an access token. Once you sign in, the model calls use your own quota.

👉 Try Workflow1111, or duplicate the Space and start rewiring it for your own use case.

All the media pipelines are built from the same four operator kinds covered in our last post and the official guide. Each node on the canvas wraps one operator, and the operator's inputs and outputs become the ports you connect edges to. As a quick reference on our four operator kinds: fn is a Python function, model is a model called through InferenceClient, space is another Gradio Space, and dataset is a row from a Hub dataset.

Let's go through the pipelines one by one.

This is the core pipeline. It has the controls you'd expect from A1111's txt2img tab: negative prompt, steps, CFG, seed, width and height, plus a model_id field for choosing the checkpoint. The prompt goes through a prompt-builder fn node first, which appends the selected style preset and cleans up the text, then into a model node that calls the checkpoint through Inference Providers. A post-process fn node writes the generation parameters into the PNG's metadata on the way out, which is what the PNG Info pipeline reads back later.

In Automatic1111, hi-resolution fix first upscales the txt2img output and then runs a second denoising pass. Here it's a two-node detour instead. The text-to-image result goes into a FLUX.1-Kontext model node with a refine instruction ("enhance fine detail and micro-texture, keep the composition identical") and comes back sharper and larger.

That same Kontext node doubles as the image-to-image tab. Upload an image, describe the change you want, and it returns the edited image.

Start with a rough prompt like "A lighthouse in a storm." This pipeline sends it to a Qwen3-4B model node, and a small fn node turns the reply into a clean list of tags, capped at forty: "stormy sea, wet rocks, dramatic composition, low angle shot, volumetric lighting, ominous tone." You can connect any diffusion model node to this output to render the image.

There's no custom node involved, unlike in ComfyUI. In a Gradio workflow the LLM and the diffusion model are both ordinary model operators on the same canvas.

This is like AUTOMATIC1111's Interrogate button, with a VLM doing the interrogating instead of CLIP. Qwen2.5-VL looks at a night-market photo and writes a prompt that could have produced it. A ViT classifier node reads the same image and returns labels: restaurant 51.9%, tobacco shop 15.6%, toyshop 9.1%.

Both nodes use the same image input, so gr.Workflow runs them in parallel and you get both answers in roughly the time it takes to run one.

AUTOMATIC1111 makes you paint an inpaint mask by hand. This pipeline generates one from a detector instead. DETR finds six objects in a street photo (three people, a dog, a bicycle, and a car), and from there the workflow splits into two branches: one draws the detected boxes on the original image, the other turns them into a mask you can feed into an inpaint pipeline downstream.

The drawing and the mask creation both happen locally with Pillow and NumPy. Only the detection call leaves the machine.

This is like AUTOMATIC1111's prompt matrix. A base prompt, "a lone oak tree," gets combined with four suffixes (at sunrise, in a thunderstorm, under the Milky Way, in autumn fog) by a fn node, and each variant goes to its own text-to-image node. A final node stitches the four results into one contact sheet.

gr.Workflow has no loop operator, so the four text-to-image nodes sit side by side on the canvas. Since they're at the same dependency depth they run in parallel, and all four images start generating at once.

This is like the Extras tab in Automatic1111. There are two upscaler nodes, and they take different routes. The first is a local Lanczos resample in an fn node, which needs no network call and finishes as fast as Pillow can resize. The second is AuraSR ×4, and it's the first space node on the canvas: it calls a Space on the Hub and treats the result like any other node output.

Background removal works the same way. BRIA RMBG-2.0 is another space node, so the whole model lives in its own Space and this canvas just calls it in.

Canny, line art, sketch, luma-depth, and posterize are the preprocessors you'd normally get from the ControlNet extension in Automatic1111. Here, each one is a fn node written in plain NumPy, with no model behind it. On a pre-loaded example photo of a building facade, each annotator takes about half a second on CPU.

There are 36 operator nodes in the app, 32 are fn nodes, and 22 of those run entirely in-process without a network call. Roughly two-thirds of the canvas keeps working if you lose your connection. Since these are regular Python functions, you can also test them directly, with no canvas, server, or GPU involved.

AUTOMATIC1111 stores generation details in the PNG's parameters text chunk, and the PNG Info tab reads them back. Workflow1111 does the same. The post-process node on the text-to-image pipeline writes the metadata, and this pipeline reads it back out, including the prompt, negative prompt, steps, CFG, seed, image size, and model.

The image node that PNG Info reads from also feeds a Wan 2.2 I2V A14B node, which animates it; in the demo example a sleeping fox wakes up and starts moving. There's no second upload box because one reference node can feed as many downstream pipelines as you need, so a single upload gets its metadata read and gets animated on the same canvas.

So far every model call has gone to someone else's hardware, through Inference Providers or a Space. That's why you can build and run something like Workflow1111 without a GPU of your own.

A fn node is just Python, though, so it can equally load a model locally and run it on your own GPU. FastVideo/fastvideo-fasth3-preview is a gr.Workflow app that does exactly that. It runs FastH3, a four-step distillation of MiniMax-H3, and generates video with a soundtrack on ZeroGPU.

The whole app comes down to one bound function:

ZeroGPU gives the function a GPU when it needs one, then releases it when the call is done. gr.Workflow doesn't need to know about any of that. It just calls the fn node.

This isn't specific to Spaces either. Point bind= to a function that loads a local checkpoint, run .launch() on your own machine, and the Workflow1111 canvas can drive your own GPU.

Every output node on the canvas becomes a REST endpoint, with no routes written by hand. Workflow1111 exposes nine of them: /image, /edited_image, /generated_prompt, /recovered_prompt, /detected_objects, /x_y_grid, /upscaled_local, /annotator_map, and /png_info.

The same endpoints are also MCP tools. Launch with mcp_server=True (guide) and every output node shows up as a tool an AI assistant can call. Point Claude Code, Cursor, or any MCP client at the server URL:

Now an agent can generate an image, read a prompt back out, or run detection as steps in a larger task, with no glue code. Each caller sends their own token in the X-HF-Token header, so the Space holds none of its own.

AUTOMATIC1111 gave us the feature list, but the tool Gradio Workflow really gets compared to is ComfyUI, since both are node graphs. For a lot of what people want to build and ship, gr.Workflow covers the same ground.

The result is a multi-model pipeline that people can open in a browser, sign into, use right away, and call from code.

Workflow1111 has 73 nodes, but it started with just this:

bind= turns your functions into nodes, edges= connects them, and .launch() opens the canvas in your browser so you can keep editing there. When it's ready, gradio deploy puts the whole thing on a Space. The gr.Workflow guide has the full details, including the JSON schema and every operator type.

If you'd rather start from something that already works, open Workflow1111, hit Duplicate, and pick one of the eleven pipelines to change: delete nodes, swap models, rewire the flow. If you'd rather start smaller, the previous post has five workflows you can get running in about a minute each.

Whatever you build, post it on X and tag @gradio. We'd be happy to amplify your workflows.

4-step MiniMax-H3 — video with a matching soundtrack

Automatic1111-style studio on one gr.Workflow canvas

Really impressive breakdown the part that stands out most is how the graph structure gives you free parallelism (the prompt-matrix and interrogate examples) without any extra orchestration code. The mix of fn, model, and space node types on one canvas also makes the ComfyUI comparison land well: you get custom-node flexibility from plain Python, but zero-code REST/MCP endpoints for free. Curious how complex a canvas can get before performance or maintainability becomes a concern has anyone pushed past 73 nodes

Analisis yang sangat mengesankan, bagian yang paling menonjol adalah bagaimana struktur graf memberikan paralelisme gratis (contoh prompt-matrix dan interrogate) tanpa kode orkestrasi tambahan. Perpaduan tipe node fn, model, dan space pada satu kanvas juga membuat perbandingan dengan ComfyUI tepat: Anda mendapatkan fleksibilitas node kustom dari Python biasa, tetapi endpoint REST/MCP tanpa kode secara gratis. Saya penasaran seberapa kompleks sebuah kanvas dapat dibuat sebelum kinerja atau pemeliharaan menjadi masalah, apakah ada yang pernah melampaui 73 node?

Agent skills capture repeatable engineering work in files teams can review and reuse, while tools, project context, and permissions remain specific to the host that runs them.

How many times this week did you re-explain the same task to an agent? How many times did you ask your colleague with deep institutional knowledge how to solve a specific problem? That context shouldn’t be lost in a chat or locked in one person’s head. Agent skills let you capture repeatable instructions so you and your agents can reuse them. The skill you write for yourself tonight can later become part of a team’s pipeline.

An agent skill is a versioned directory centered on a SKILL.md file that describes when and how to do a repeatable task. You can share those instructions across agents, but the environment still needs to provide the tools, credentials, and permissions to carry them out. A skill can describe how to query a database, for example, but it doesn’t grant access to that database.

I covered this topic live with Shishir Tewari, Senior Manager, Data Engineering at Procore, during GitHub Universe 2026. Our session was titled “Build once, run on any agent: a practical guide to agent skills”.

A skill works best when it has a clear job, input, and output. For example, let’s say you’re building an agent that checks AI-generated changes against the original request. If the same agent assesses its own work, its explanation might influence the review. With Proof Agent, we use a separate verifier to examine the changes and provide evidence for its findings. The skill’s frontmatter names the task and describes its purpose:

At the center is a simple rule: self-verification is not verification.

The When to Verify section in Proof Agent’s SKILL.md says when to invoke the skill. The remaining instructions explain what the verifier reviews and what evidence to include in its findings.

When the judgment that makes a data pipeline correct lives in four different people’s heads, those four people are the roadmap. Each change to the pipeline depends on their availability and knowledge of the data. Data Forge is an example of how to capture parts of that judgment in skills that work together.

In the support-desk pipeline example, we start with a request for metrics that count incidents created and resolved. Before building the pipeline, the forge-init skill discovers details such as source tables and naming conventions, then writes them to a resolved manifest. The other skills read that manifest for the project context they need.

The forge-builder skill then coordinates the work from the issue through to a pull request. It uses forge-dbx to query the data platform and forge-lint to apply the team’s standards as it designs and builds the pipeline. A person reviews the proposed decisions along the way, and the resulting pull request contains the pipeline code, schema changes, and tests.

Each skill has a defined responsibility, and they share project context instead of rediscovering it independently. When a step changes, you can change one skill and leave the rest alone.

Skills fit bounded, repeatable work that benefits from reusable judgment, such as a checklist, release, migration, or metric pipeline. If a workflow needs a stable interface, shared state, an audit trail, long-running control, or permissions enforced outside the model, an application is a better fit.

We don’t want to hardcode every project’s names, database, or conventions into the skills. In the Data Forge support-desk example, a manifest describes the project, metric store, and platform so the skills can use the right project details without baking them into their instructions:

With the discovered details in the resolved manifest, the other skills don’t have to make their own assumptions about the project.

Keep discovered project details separate from team standards. The forge-init initialization skill can inspect existing schemas and code patterns; the forge-lint skill supplies the rules to follow before code is generated. A pattern found in a repository isn’t automatically a rule to preserve, so make discovered details reviewable and let people confirm or change them where business judgment is needed. To check portability, ask: could another team use these skills with its own manifest without rewriting them?

The forge-dbx skill gives the other Data Forge skills one way to access the data platform. It reads the manifest and selects a Databricks or DuckDB adapter, so each skill doesn’t need its own connection and query logic.

The manifest can choose DuckDB for the local support-desk demo, but it can’t install the DuckDB CLI or grant database access. Those remain setup responsibilities for the environment and its user. The manifest picks the engine; the host provides the access.

The Data Forge support-desk workflow has seven phases, with a human checkpoint at each one. The workflow overview shows how the skills fit together. Before a phase proceeds, the workflow checks that the previous phase is complete; before schema changes run, it asks for approval.

The Proof Agent example applies the same principle to code review. A GitHub Actions workflow gives the verifier the original request and code changes, but not the coding agent’s own assessment. The verifier returns PASS, FAIL, or PARTIAL and must cite evidence in the changed files. The GitHub Action does a static review of the diff; it doesn’t execute code or run tests. In the demo workflow, we set block-on-fail: false so findings were advisory. By default, a FAIL fails the check, which blocks the merge if the check is required. The aim is to keep test results and merge requirements in your repository’s CI checks and rules.

Supporting multiple clients can mean keeping several copies of the same instructions in sync. In the Data Forge example, we keep skills/*/SKILL.md as the source and use a packaging script to generate client-specific files: .claude-plugin/plugin.json for Claude Code, .cursor-plugin/plugin.json for Cursor, and .github/agents/*.agent.md for GitHub Copilot. The script also includes a check mode for CI:

Clients can differ in their available models, tools, credentials, and permissions. After installing a skill, check that the client recognizes it for the intended task, loads its references, can use the required tools, and returns the evidence the skill calls for.

Start with the task you’re tired of explaining. Write down what it needs, where it stops, and what a reviewer sees. Then try it with another agent and improve it as you learn what works.

#9903. FCC proposes 'tit-for-tat' restrictions on foreign satellite operators

December vote would launch rulemaking to mirror barriers facing US providers abroad, with EU spectrum plans in the crosshairs

The US Federal Communications Commission (FCC) will vote in December on proposals [PDF] that would restrict foreign satellite operators in the same way their home countries restrict US providers.

The telecoms regulator says the move is to "ensure reciprocity and fair dealing" in the rules governing satellite operators. The main aim appears to be hitting back at European efforts to build up the region's own space communications industries.

According to the FCC, the US has so far welcomed satellite systems licensed abroad on a level playing field, but that regulators elsewhere have begun holding US systems to different rules than they apply to their own domestic suppliers.

"This has operated to the disadvantage of American satellite providers that are or may be burdened with regulatory and spectrum limitations that their competitors in foreign nations simply do not face," said FCC chairman Brendan Carr.

The FCC has singled out the EU's Digital Networks Act, which proposes harmonized connectivity rules across the bloc. A separate proposal would overhaul authorization for mobile satellite services (MSS) in the 2 GHz band after existing rights expire in May 2027.

Earlier this year, the FCC laid out some of its concerns, saying that EU-wide authorization of satellite spectrum would replace the national licensing by member states "with which US satellite operators have become accustomed," and could require wholesale relicensing of any US systems operating in Europe.

"The FCC voting on foreign satellite companies is consistent with the Digital Networks Act, but is more of a response to the EU's decisions on how it plans to allocate the EU-wide 2 GHz spectrum," CCS Insight analyst Joe Gardiner told The Register.

"The EU outlined in its proposal that, for two-thirds of the spectrum, only operators based in the EU with EU ownership and aligned with the EU's strategic goals will be considered for the spectrum.

"This has locked out companies like SpaceX and Amazon Leo from attaining access to spectrum that is highly valuable for satellite direct-to-device services. The US government is looking to retaliate, to support the US constellations that would have attempted to win this EU-wide spectrum."

Following an initial consultation in March, the FCC will vote in December on opening a rulemaking to reconsider how foreign-licensed satellite operators gain access to the US market.

"It is time for this regulatory asymmetry to end," Carr said, adding that the FCC now proposes to mirror any regulations that foreign nations apply to American satellite providers.

"If there are limits or restrictions on American providers operating abroad, then the notice proposes to apply those or similar regulatory restraints to satellite providers from those countries that are operating here."

Britain is outside the EU, but does not escape the FCC's ire. The agency previously claimed the UK Space Agency allocates a significant portion of its budget, circa 75 percent in 2023/24, to European Space Agency (ESA) procurements, which US companies are not allowed to bid for as America is not a member of ESA.

British satellite operators could therefore face restrictions on access to the US market if the FCC adopts reciprocal measures. The UK's space industry generated £18.6 billion in income in 2022/23, according to the UK Space Agency. ®
